pages.metaTitle: Present Continuous vs Present Simple ESL Lesson Plan (A2)
pages.description: Free 60-minute A2 ESL lesson plan on the present continuous vs present simple: aims, language analysis, timed stages, printable handouts and a full answer key.
pages.keywords: present continuous vs present simple lesson plan, present continuous vs present simple ESL lesson, teaching the present continuous vs present simple, A2 ESL lesson plan, ESA boomerang lesson plan, free ESL lesson plans
pages.teaches: Present Continuous vs Present Simple (English grammar)

hero.text: A complete 60-minute lesson on the present continuous vs present simple for A2 classes, built on the ESA boomerang framework, with photocopiable handouts and an answer key.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: Elementary students who can use the present simple for routines and know common action verbs. Most have met the present continuous but confuse it with the present simple and often leave out *be*.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis to read before you teach, a stage-by-stage procedure with timings and interaction patterns, and the handouts and answer key at the end, ready to print.

items.definition: A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, drop the personalised extension in Activate 2 and keep the cafe game to a single round.
Speaking and reading, with some writing
The present continuous for actions happening now, contrasted with the present simple for routines
ESA boomerang (Engage, Activate, Study, Activate)

Handout 1 (text messages), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3A and 3B (café scene cards for the information gap), a busy photo for the Engage stage (any market or street photo projected or printed, or a board sketch).
About 15 minutes: print Handouts 1 and 2 per learner, and Handouts 3A and 3B so that each pair has one of each. Find a busy street or market photo, or be ready to sketch one.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To clarify and practise the present continuous for actions happening now, contrasted with the present simple for routines.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can describe what people are doing at the moment and contrast it with what they usually do, e.g. *He usually walks to work, but today he's taking a taxi.*
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in describing scenes.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise reading for specific information (text messages).
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise *-ing* spelling rules.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
Yes, she is. / No, she isn't.
Yes, they are. / No, they aren't.
blocks.heading: Form
Form: notes
text: Spelling of *-ing*:
bullets: Most verbs add *-ing*: read → reading, play → playing.
Verbs ending in *-e* drop the *e*: make → making, write → writing.
One vowel + one consonant (stressed) doubles the consonant: sit → sitting, run → running, swim → swimming.
*-ie* → *-ying*: lie → lying, die → dying.

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
bullets: **Present continuous:** actions happening at the moment of speaking or around now: *Look! It's raining. I'm reading a good book this week.*
**Present simple:** routines, habits and permanent facts: *I take the bus every day.*
**Contrast:** *He usually walks to work, but today he's taking a taxi.*
Time words: *now, right now, at the moment, today, this week, Look! Listen!* vs *every day, usually, always, often, on Mondays*.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Contractions are normal in speech: *I'm /aɪm/, she's /ʃiːz/, they're /ðeə/*.
*-ing* is pronounced /ɪŋ/ with no hard /g/ at the end.
In questions, *are* is weak: *What are you doing?* /wɒt ə jə ˈduːɪŋ/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***Ravi is taking a taxi today.*** Is Ravi in the taxi now? (Yes.) · Does he take a taxi every day? (No.) · Is this a habit? (No, it's just today / now.)
***Ravi usually walks to work.*** Does he walk most days? (Yes.) · Is he walking now? (We don't know / not necessarily.)

rows: Board the three parts in separate boxes: subject + be + verb-ing. Use a finger-counting gesture: three fingers for *He – is – reading*.
Using the continuous for routines (*I am going to school every day*).
Use the timeline contrast and highlight time words. Students sort time words into two columns.
Quick spelling race on the board in Study; add the spelling rules box to Handout 2.
Students run out of ideas in Activate 1.
Provide the prompt questions on the board: *Who? What are they doing? Where?*
Info-gap students look at each other's cards.
Seat pairs back to back or ask them to hold the card up close and not show it.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: NOW: now, at the moment, today, this week, Look!, Listen! · EVERY DAY: usually, always, often, every day, on Mondays
Timeline: routine (x x x x) vs NOW (~~~). He usually **walks** to work. Today he**'s taking** a taxi. subject + am/is/are + verb**-ing**. Negative: isn't / aren't. Question: Is he ...? Are they ...?
make → making · sit → sitting · lie → lying · play → playing
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Present Continuous vs Present Simple, step by step

stages.name: Engage
text: **Aim:** To create interest in the topic and get students talking about actions in a scene.

Show a busy market or street photo (or sketch a simple scene on the board: a man on a phone, a girl running, a woman buying fruit). Say: *"Look at this photo. Where is it? Is it busy?"* Take two or three quick answers.
Say: *"Look for 30 seconds. Then close your eyes."* After 30 seconds, hide the photo. Ask: *"How many people can you remember? What are they doing?"* Accept any answers and do not correct grammar.
Ask: *"Are you a busy person? What do you usually do on Saturday morning?"* Students tell a partner in one minute.
**Transition:** *"OK, now let's try a speaking game."*

stages.name: Activate 1, first try
text: **Aim:** To let students use the language they have in a communicative task, and to diagnose what they need.

Give out Handout 3A to Student A and Handout 3B to Student B in each pair. Say: *"This is a café. You have a card with eight people. Your partner has a different card. Don't show your partner! Tell your partner what people are doing. Find the differences. You have four minutes."*
ICQs: *"Can you show your card?"* (No.) *"What do you find?"* (Differences.)
Students try the task. **Do not help or correct.** Monitor and write down: (a) sentences without *be*; (b) wrong use of present simple; (c) good sentences.

Stop after four minutes. Ask: *"How many differences did you find?"* Collect a number from each pair. Say: *"Keep your cards. We will do this again later."* Collect the cards or ask students to turn them over.
**Transition:** *"Let's look at some messages. They will help us with the language."*

stages.name: Study, reading and language focus
text: **Aim:** To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the present continuous and contrast it with the present simple.
Give out Handout 1. **Reading task:** *"Read the four messages. Where is each person? Write the place. Two minutes."* Students check in pairs, then check as a class. (Answers in the Answer Key.)
**Noticing:** *"Underline the verbs that end in -ing."* Elicit: *I'm sitting, It's raining, We're having, She's taking ...*
**Meaning.** Write on the board: *Ravi usually walks to work. Today he's taking a taxi.* Draw a timeline: crosses for every day, a wavy line at NOW. Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
**Form.** Elicit the three parts: subject + am / is / are + verb-ing. Elicit the negative and the question from the messages. Write the form table on the board.
**Spelling.** Write *make, sit, lie, play* on the board. Students come to the board and write the *-ing* form. Elicit the rules.
**Time words.** Students sort the time words (Handout 2, Exercise A) into two columns with a partner. Check quickly.
**Pronunciation.** Drill chorally and individually with contractions: *I'm sitting on the bus. She's taking a taxi. What are you doing?* Model the weak form of *are*.
**Error feedback from Activate 1.** Board two or three errors you noted in Stage 2 (e.g. *The man reading a newspaper*). Students correct them in pairs.

stages.name: Study, controlled practice
text: **Aim:** To give accurate written practice of the form and the contrast.
Students complete Handout 2, Exercises B and C, individually. Say: *"Exercise B: choose the correct form. Exercise C: write the -ing form. Six minutes."*
ICQs: *"In B, do you write or circle?"* (Circle.) *"Alone or in pairs?"* (Alone, then check.)
Monitor and help weaker students by pointing back to the time words.
Pairs compare answers. Nominate students to read answers aloud and explain choices: *"Every day, so present simple."*

stages.name: Activate 2, second try
text: **Aim:** To give students the chance to repeat the communicative task with improved accuracy and confidence, then to personalise the language.
Students change partners (Student A works with a new Student B). Return the café cards. Say: *"Do the café game again. Use the language from today. You have five minutes."*
Monitor and note improvements. Stop when most pairs have found all six differences. Ask: *"Did you find more differences this time? Was it easier?"*

**Personalised extension (8 minutes):** Write on the board: *What are you doing this week / this month that is different from usual?* Model: *"I usually drink coffee, but this week I'm drinking green tea."* In groups of three, students tell each other two things they usually do and one thing they are doing differently this week.
Each group reports one interesting sentence about a group member to the class.

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To consolidate the lesson and give feedback.
Board four sentences heard in Activate 2: two correct, two with errors. Pairs decide which are correct and fix the others.
Ask: *"What's different between Activate 1 and Activate 2?"* Elicit that students used *be + -ing* more accurately.
Set homework.

blocks.homework: Take or find a photo of a busy place. Write 6 sentences about what is happening, and 2 sentences about what usually happens there. *Example: A man is selling mangoes. Two boys are playing. On Sundays, this market is usually very busy.*
blocks.caption: ESA boomerang (Engage, Activate, Study, Activate). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students a verb list for the café task: *carry, drink, read, talk, eat, write, sleep, wait, pay, laugh*. Allow them to write two sentences before speaking in Activate 2.

Stronger students add a reason or a contrast: *She's drinking tea because she usually doesn't sleep well after coffee.* They write a short text message describing what they are doing right now, including one contrast with their routine.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Run the cafe information gap down the rows: the learner in front holds card A, the learner behind holds card B. Nobody moves. Take one difference from each of six pairs rather than from all.
Draw the cafe on the board as eight stick figures, then rub out and change six details for the second round. The messages in Handout 1 can be read aloud twice while learners note the place only.
Send cards A and B by private message so partners cannot see each other's. Breakout rooms of two for both Activate stages, and screen-share the photo for the Engage stage.
With young learners, replace the cafe with a playground and act the differences out instead of writing them. With adults, set the second Activate stage in a workplace and let them use their own jobs.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students are successful if they: use *be + verb-ing* with the correct form of *be* in most sentences in Activate 2; choose the present simple for routines and the continuous for now in Handout 2 (8 out of 10 or better); find more differences, with fewer errors, in Activate 2 than in Activate 1.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Was the difference between Activate 1 and Activate 2 clear to me and to the students? Which errors from Activate 1 disappeared? Which remained? Did Study take too long? What would I cut next time?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Messages
text: **Read the messages. Where is each person? Write the place.**
**Find and write:**
bullets: Two things that are happening now in Dilini's message: ___________________________
Something Dilini usually does: ___________________________
Why is Dad cooking tonight? ___________________________

blocks.title: The text
text: **Dilini, 8.15 am:** Hi! I'm sitting on the bus. It's raining and the traffic is terrible! Everyone is looking at their phones. I usually walk to school, but today I'm late.
**Kasun, 1.30 pm:** We're having lunch in the canteen. Ruwan is eating his third samosa! The teachers aren't here today because they're having a meeting.
**Mum, 6.00 pm:** I'm in the supermarket. They're cleaning the floor, so it's very slow. Do we need milk? Your father is cooking dinner tonight because I'm working late.
**Ashan, 9.45 pm:** I'm not watching the match. I'm doing my homework in my room. My brother is playing loud music again. Help!

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Write the time words in the correct column.**
*now · every day · at the moment · usually · today · on Mondays · this week · always · Look! · often*
**B. Circle the correct form.**
**C. Write the -ing form.**

Listen! Someone **sings / is singing** in the garden.

**Write the differences:**

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: Intermediate students who know the basic forms of both present tenses but are unsure about temporary vs permanent situations, changing trends and stative verbs.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis to read before you teach, a stage-by-stage procedure with timings and interaction patterns, and the handouts and answer key at the end, ready to print.

items.definition: B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, give each group two trend cards instead of a full set and take one report per group.
Reading and speaking
Present simple for permanent situations against present continuous for temporary ones and changing trends, and the stative verbs that stay simple
Guided Discovery
Handout 1 (three profiles), Handout 2 (discovery task), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (trend discussion cards, cut up).
About 15 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3 per learner, and cut up one set of trend cards (Handout 4) per group of three or four.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To help students discover and practise the use of the present simple for permanent situations and the present continuous for temporary situations and changing trends, and to recognise stative verbs.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can describe permanent and temporary situations in their lives, talk about trends in their town and avoid stative verbs in the continuous.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To practise reading for specific information.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in discussing trends and expressing opinions.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: I **live** in Colombo. She **works** for a bank.
I**'m staying** with my aunt this month.
More people **are working** from home. Prices **are rising**.
I **know** the answer. This bag **belongs** to me.
blocks.heading: Form and use
Stative verbs
bullets: **Mind / opinion:** know, believe, understand, think (= have an opinion), remember, mean, agree
**Feelings:** like, love, hate, want, prefer, need
**Possession:** have (= own), own, belong
**Senses / appearance:** seem, look (= appear), taste, smell, sound

blocks.heading: Verbs with two meanings
bullets: *I think it's a good idea.* (opinion: stative) vs *I'm thinking about moving.* (mental process: dynamic)
*She has a car.* (possession) vs *She's having lunch.* (activity)
*I see what you mean.* (understand) vs *I'm seeing the doctor tomorrow.* (meeting)

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Contractions in speech: *I'm staying, they're working*.
Stress on the contrast words: *I USUALLY live in Kandy, but THIS month I'm staying in Colombo.*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***I'm staying with my aunt this month.*** Is this my permanent home? (No.) · Is it true now? (Yes.) · Will it change? (Yes, probably soon.)
***I know the answer.*** Is knowing an action you can see? (No, it's a state.) · Can we say *I'm knowing*? (No.)

rows: Stative verbs in the continuous (*I'm knowing, I'm wanting*).
Card sort in the discovery task; keep a stative verb list on the board for the whole lesson.
Show the meaning pairs side by side; CCQ: *Is it an opinion or an activity?*
Students find the discovery questions hard.
Monitor and give the first answer for one example; allow pairs to compare with another pair.
Give the sentence starters on Handout 4.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: know, believe, understand, want, need, like, love, hate, prefer, belong, own, seem, mean

PERMANENT → present simple: I live in Colombo. · TEMPORARY → present continuous: I'm staying with my aunt this month. · CHANGING TRENDS → continuous: More people are working from home. · STATES → simple only: I know. (not I'm knowing)
think: opinion vs process · have: own vs activity · see: understand vs meet
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: State Verbs, step by step

stages.name: Lead-in
text: **Aim:** To generate interest and personalise the topic.
Write on the board: *Always true about me* and *Different at the moment*. Model: *"I always drink tea in the morning. At the moment, I'm learning to swim."*
Students tell a partner one thing for each column (2 minutes).
Take two or three examples from the class. Write one of each on the board without comment. These will be used later.

stages.name: Context, reading
text: **Aim:** To present the target language in context and check understanding.
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read about three people. Whose life is changing the most? Three minutes."*
Students read and decide. Pairs compare. Take a class vote and ask for reasons.
**Detail task:** Students answer the three questions under the profiles. Check as a class.

stages.name: Discovery task
text: **Aim:** To guide students to work out the rules for themselves.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Look at the sentences from the texts. Answer the questions with your partner. Don't use a grammar book! Think about the meaning."*
ICQs: *"Do you work alone?"* (No, in pairs.) *"Do I give you the rules?"* (No, we find them.)
Pairs work through Part A (permanent / temporary / trends) and Part B (stative verbs sort).
Monitor. If pairs are stuck, ask a guiding question: *"Is Tharindu's job in Melbourne forever?"*
When most pairs have finished, pair up the pairs to compare answers (2 minutes).

stages.name: Check and clarify
text: **Aim:** To confirm the rules and clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
Elicit the answers to Part A. Build the rules on the centre of the board as students give them.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
Elicit the stative verbs from Part B and board them on the left. Ask: *"Why is I'm knowing wrong?"*
Show the verb pairs (think, have, see). Ask: *"Which one is an opinion? Which is an activity?"*
Return to the students' sentences from the lead-in on the board. Ask: *"Are these correct? Why?"*
Drill the contrast sentence with stress: *I USUALLY live in Kandy, but THIS month I'm staying in Colombo.*

stages.name: Controlled practice
text: **Aim:** To practise choosing the correct form accurately.
Give out Handout 3. Students complete Exercise A (10 items) individually (5 minutes).
In pairs, they compare and justify each answer using the rules: *"Temporary, so continuous."*
Check as a class. For each stative verb, ask: *"Why not the continuous?"*
Fast finishers do Exercise B (error correction).

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.time: 15 min · Groups of three or four
text: **Aim:** To use the target language fluently in a discussion about trends and opinions.

Give each group a set of trend cards (Handout 4). Model with one card: *"Online shopping. In my town, more people are shopping online. My mother still goes to the market every day. I believe online shopping is convenient, but I don't think it's good for small shops."*
Say: *"Take a card. Talk for one minute: what is changing in your town? What do you think about it? Use the sentence starters."* Each student takes at least two cards.
Monitor and note examples of good use and errors (especially stative verbs).
Each group chooses the most interesting trend and reports it to the class in two or three sentences.

stages.name: Feedback
text: **Aim:** To give feedback on language from the freer practice.
Board three errors and two good sentences from your notes. Pairs correct the errors.
Elicit the four rules one last time without looking at the board.
Set homework.

blocks.homework: Write a 120-word paragraph: *My life at the moment.* Include two permanent facts, three temporary situations, one trend in your town and two opinions using stative verbs.
blocks.caption: Guided Discovery. Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Highlight the key time words (*this month, at the moment, these days*) on Handout 1 before reading. Let weaker students do Part A of the discovery task only, then copy Part B from the board.

Ask stronger students to find two verbs on Handout 3 that change meaning in the continuous, and write a pair of sentences for each. In the discussion, they must use *these days, nowadays, more and more*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the discovery task in pairs but check it with the whole class from the board rather than pairing pairs. For the trend discussion, give each row one card instead of a set, and take one report from each row.

Put the three profiles on the board one at a time, each in four or five sentences. Read the trend topics aloud as a list; learners choose one and talk, with the sentence starters written on the board.
Use a shared document for the discovery task so you can watch the rules appear and correct a wrong one early. Breakout rooms of three for the trends, with one card pasted into each room's chat.

With young learners, drop the trends and keep the temporary and permanent contrast with their own lives this week. With adults, use trends in their own trade or profession, which usually produces better examples than the cards.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students can explain (in their own words) when to use each tense. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A. In the discussion, students avoid stative verbs in the continuous.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Were the guiding questions clear enough for students to find the rules? Did any pairs discover the rules incorrectly? How did I handle it? How well did students use stative verbs in the discussion?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Changing Lives
text: **Read the three profiles. Whose life is changing the most?**
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: Where does Tharindu come from? Where is he living now? ___________________________
What is changing about Nadeesha's company? ___________________________
What trend does Mr Fernando talk about? ___________________________

blocks.title: The text
text: **Tharindu, 22, student**

Tharindu comes from Galle, but this year he's studying engineering in Melbourne. He's sharing a flat with two other students from India. "I love the city, but I miss my mother's cooking," he says. "I'm learning to cook, slowly! Life here is expensive, and prices are going up every month, so I'm working part-time in a café at the weekends."
**Nadeesha, 35, marketing manager**

Nadeesha works for a big company in Colombo. Before, she spent two hours a day in traffic. Now, like many people, she's working from home three days a week. "My company is changing the way it works," she explains. "More and more meetings are happening online. I don't know if it's better, but I have more time for my children."
**Mr Fernando, 68, retired teacher**

Mr Fernando lives in a village near Kurunegala. He taught English for forty years. These days, he's teaching his grandchildren to read, and he's writing a book about the history of his village. "Young people are leaving the village for the cities," he says. "I understand why, but it makes me sad."

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Discovery Task
text: **Part A. Look at these sentences from the profiles.**
**Answer the questions with your partner.**
**Part B. Look at these verbs from the profiles. Can we use them in the -ing form here? Sort them.**
*love · miss · learn · know · understand · work · have (= own) · cook · teach · write*
**Part C. Think!**
bullets: Tharindu **comes** from Galle.

Which tense do we use for temporary situations and trends? ___________________________
Find the time words in the profiles that go with the temporary situations: ___________________________
Nadeesha says *I don't know*. Why not *I'm not knowing*? ___________________________
Look: *I think it's a good idea.* / *I'm thinking about moving.* What is the difference in meaning? ___________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Put the verb into the present simple or the present continuous.**
**B. Correct the mistakes. One sentence is correct.**
bullets: My brother ____________ (study) in Melbourne this year.
This bag ____________ (belong) to my teacher.

text: **Sentence starters**

hero.text: A complete 60-minute lesson on the present continuous with always for B2 classes, built on the TTT framework, with photocopiable handouts and an answer key.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: Upper-intermediate students who are confident with basic present tenses. They have rarely used *always* + continuous for complaints, and they are inconsistent with verbs that have both stative and dynamic meanings.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis to read before you teach, a stage-by-stage procedure with timings and interaction patterns, and the handouts and answer key at the end, ready to print.

items.definition: B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, run only the first role-play scenario in Test 2 and skip the performance to the class.
Speaking and reading
Always with the present continuous for annoying habits, get plus comparative for gradual change, be being for temporary behaviour, and stative against dynamic meanings
TTT (Test, Teach, Test)
Handout 1 (Test 1), Handout 2 (blog: Things My Flatmate Does), Handout 3 (Teach: language reference and practice), Handout 4 (role-play cards for Test 2).
About 15 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3 per learner and one set of role-play cards (Handout 4) per pair. Read Test 1 through first so you can mark the class list quickly while monitoring.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To diagnose and develop students' use of present forms for (a) annoying habits (*always* + continuous), (b) gradual change (*getting* + comparative), (c) stative/dynamic verb meanings and (d) the present simple for timetables.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can make a polite but honest complaint about someone's habits, using *always* + continuous and appropriate softening language.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency and appropriate intonation in a polite complaint role-play.
**Subsidiary aim.** To read a blog for writer's attitude.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: She **always borrows** books from the library.
I **see** what you mean. She **has** a car. This **tastes** good.
I**'m seeing** the doctor at 4. She**'s having** a hard time. The chef **is tasting** the sauce.
blocks.heading: Form, meaning and use
Pronunciation
bullets: *always* + continuous: the main stress falls on *always*, often with a fall-rise to show irritation: *He's ALways leaving the lights on!*
Softening language is stressed less and spoken more quickly: *It's just that ..., I don't know if you've noticed, but ...*

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***He's always leaving dirty dishes in the sink.*** Does it happen often? (Yes, very often, maybe too often.) · How does the speaker feel? (Annoyed.) · Does it really happen every single time? (Probably not; the speaker is exaggerating.)
***You're being very quiet today.*** Are you usually quiet? (No.) · Is it just your behaviour today? (Yes.)

rows: Word order: *He always is losing his keys.*
Show the position on the board: be + always + verb-ing.
Overuse of *always* + continuous making complaints sound rude.
Teach softening language (*I've noticed that ..., It's just that ...*) before the role-play.
Give pairs of sentences and ask: *Can you own it? Is it an activity?*
Test 1 is too difficult for some students and they lose confidence.
Tell students clearly before Test 1 that it is a diagnostic and that mistakes are useful.
Teach stage expands to cover everything.
Use the Test 1 results: teach only items that more than a third of the class got wrong.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: always + continuous = annoyance: She's always borrowing ... · getting + comparative = change: It's getting hotter. · being + adjective = temporary behaviour · stative vs dynamic: have, see, think, taste · timetable: The bus leaves at 8.
I've noticed that ... · It's just that ... · I don't mean to complain, but ... · Would you mind ...? · Could you try to ...?
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Present Continuous with Always, step by step

stages.name: Lead-in
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic of annoying habits and engage students personally.
Say: *"Think about people on buses, in class, at home or online. What habits annoy you?"* Give one example without using the target language: *"People who talk loudly on the phone on the bus."*
Students list three annoying habits with a partner (2 minutes).
Take ideas from the class and board key words only (*phone, late, borrow, noise*). Do not focus on grammar.

stages.name: Test 1
text: **Aim:** To diagnose what students already know and what they need.
Say: *"Before I teach anything, I want to see what you know. This is not an exam, and mistakes are very useful for me. Work alone, no dictionaries. Seven minutes."* Give out Handout 1.
ICQs: *"Can you work with a partner?"* (No.) *"Is it a problem if you make mistakes?"* (No.)
Monitor closely. Note on a class list which items cause problems for many students.
When most students have finished, stop. Do not give answers.

stages.name: Diagnose
text: **Aim:** To identify the language the class needs to focus on.
Pairs compare their answers and discuss any differences (2 minutes).
Go through the items quickly. For each, ask: *"Who has A? Who has B?"* Count hands. **Do not confirm answers yet.**
Board the numbers of the two or three items where the class disagreed most (left of the board). Say: *"These are our focus today."*

stages.name: Teach
text: **Aim:** To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the problem areas identified in Test 1.
**Context.** Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Read the blog. How does the writer feel about her flatmate? Do you think she's being fair?"* (3 minutes.) Elicit that she is annoyed but also funny.
**Noticing.** Students underline every present form in the blog (2 minutes).
**Clarify the problem areas.** Focus first on the items from the Diagnose stage. For each one:

**always + continuous:** Write *She's always borrowing my charger!* and *She always borrows books from the library.* Ask the CCQs. Elicit that the first shows annoyance. Board the word order: be + always + verb-ing.
**gradual change:** Write *It's getting hotter every year.* Ask: *Is it changing? Is it finished?*
**stative / dynamic:** Board pairs from the blog (*I see what you mean / I'm seeing someone*; *She has a cat / She's having a party*). Students explain the difference to a partner.
**being + adjective:** *You're being very quiet today.* CCQ: *Are you usually quiet?*
**Pronunciation.** Model the irritated intonation: *He's ALways leaving the lights on!* Students repeat chorally, then say it with different feelings (annoyed, amused).
**Quick practice.** Students do Handout 3, Exercise A (4 minutes) and check in pairs.
**Answer Test 1.** Now give the correct answers to Test 1. Students mark their own work.

stages.name: Test 2
text: **Aim:** To check improvement through a freer, communicative task.
Pairs correct their own Test 1 answers using what they learned (3 minutes).

**Prepare the role-play.** Give out Handout 4. Teach the complaint language on the right of the board. Say: *"You are flatmates. Student A has a problem with Student B's habits. Make a polite but honest complaint. Student B, respond, explain and suggest a change. Use at least three phrases from the board."*
ICQs: *"Are you angry or polite?"* (Polite but honest.) *"Who suggests a change?"* (Student B.)
Students read their cards and prepare for 2 minutes.
**Role-play 1** (4 minutes). Monitor and note language use.
Students swap roles and use the second scenario (4 minutes).
**Performance:** two or three pairs perform for the class. The class listens and notes: *How many examples of always + continuous? Was the complaint polite?*

stages.name: Feedback
text: **Aim:** To compare Test 1 and Test 2 performance and give final feedback.
Ask: *"Was it easier to use these structures in the role-play than in Test 1?"*
Board four sentences heard during the role-plays. Students identify and correct errors.
Board one or two very natural complaints and praise them.
Set homework.

blocks.homework: Write a humorous blog post (150 words) about someone's annoying habits. Use *always* + continuous at least three times, *getting* + comparative once and one stative/dynamic pair.
blocks.caption: TTT (Test, Teach, Test). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Provide sentence frames for the role-play: *I've noticed that you're always ... . Could you try to ...?* Allow weaker students to do Test 2 in a group of three, with one student as an observer.
Stronger students add sarcastic stress patterns and hedging (*a bit, kind of, sort of*). Ask them to use *forever* and *constantly* as alternatives to *always*.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Diagnose by a show of hands per item rather than by reading over shoulders, and board only the three items with the widest disagreement. Run the role-play simultaneously in fixed pairs and let three pairs perform.

Dictate the ten Test 1 items; learners write only the verb form. Read the blog aloud twice and board the four sentences the clarification needs. The role-play works from two situations written on the board.
Set Test 1 as a private-message quiz so answers arrive without learners seeing each other's. Use breakout rooms of two for the role-play and rejoin for the performance, which carries well on screen.

With teenagers, set the complaints among classmates or siblings rather than flatmates. With adults, the office scenario usually lands better than the flat; encourage real examples, kept polite about people who are not present.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Test 1 vs Test 2: students use *always* + continuous accurately and appropriately in the role-play. Students choose the correct stative or dynamic form in 4 out of 5 Teach practice items. Complaints include at least one softening phrase.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did Test 1 show clearly what the class needed? Did I keep the Teach stage focused, or did I teach things they already knew? How much better was Test 2?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Test 1
text: **Complete the sentences with an appropriate present form of the verb in brackets. Do your best: this is not an exam!**
bullets: My brother is so annoying! He ____________________ (always / leave) dirty dishes in the sink!
The planet ____________________ (get) warmer and warmer.
I ____________________ (see) what you mean, but I don't agree.
You ____________________ (be) very quiet today. Is anything wrong?
The concert ____________________ (start) at 7.30 tonight, according to the ticket.
My grandmother ____________________ (always / go) to the temple on poya days. It's her tradition.
Sorry, I can't talk now. I ____________________ (have) dinner.
This coffee ____________________ (taste) strange. Is the milk old?
I ____________________ (see) my dentist on Friday. It's my check-up.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Blog
text: **Read the blog. How does the writer feel about her flatmate? Underline all the present forms.**
**Questions**
bullets: What does the writer like about Shanika? ___________________________
Which habits annoy her? ___________________________
Why is the writer being patient at the moment? ___________________________

blocks.title: The text
text: **Things My Flatmate Does That Drive Me Crazy**
I love my flatmate, Shanika. Really, I do. She's funny, kind and she has the best cat in Colombo. But living with her is getting more difficult every week.
First, she's always borrowing my phone charger. I buy a new one, it disappears. I buy another one, it disappears too. Where do they go? Nobody knows.
Second, she's constantly singing in the shower at 6 am. She has a lovely voice, but not at 6 am!
Third, she always leaves the lights on. Our electricity bill is getting higher and higher. When I mention it, she says, "I see what you mean," and then she does it again.
At the moment she's having a difficult time at work, so I'm being patient. And tonight she's cooking dinner for me, which is very sweet. The problem is, this curry tastes a little strange ...
Am I being unfair? Tell me in the comments!

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Language Focus and Practice
text: **Language reference**
**A. Choose the best form.**
**B. Rewrite these neutral sentences as complaints.**
bullets: He **always loses / is always losing** his keys! It's so frustrating.
My father **always reads / is always reading** the newspaper at breakfast. It's his routine.
Look, the sky **gets / is getting** darker. It's going to rain.
I **have / am having** two sisters and a brother.
We **have / are having** a party on Saturday. Can you come?
You **are / are being** silly. Stop it!
This fish **smells / is smelling** bad.
I **think / am thinking** about changing jobs.
My neighbour plays loud music. → ___________________________

rows: It's getting more difficult every week.
I see what you mean. She has a cat. This tastes strange.
She's having a difficult time. I'm seeing the doctor.

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Role-play Cards (Test 2)
text: **Scenario 1: Student A** You share a flat with Student B. You are unhappy because B: leaves dishes in the sink, borrows your clothes without asking, and plays games late at night. Make a polite but honest complaint. Use *always* + continuous and softening language.

**Scenario 1: Student B** You share a flat with Student A. Listen to A's complaint. Explain your side (you are having a busy time at work, you are getting tired, etc.). Suggest one change and ask for one change from A.
**Scenario 2: Student A** You work in an office with Student B. B is a nice colleague, but B: talks loudly on the phone, takes your stapler and arrives late to meetings. Make a polite complaint.

**Scenario 2: Student B** You work with Student A. Listen to A's complaint. Explain (you are being given more work, your bus is always late, etc.). Agree to one change. Mention one habit of A's that also annoys you!
**Useful language**
bullets: *I've noticed that you're always ...*
*It's just that ...*
*I don't mean to complain, but ...*
*Would you mind not ...-ing?*
*Could you try to ...?*
*I'm sorry, I didn't realise. I'm having a really busy time at the moment.*

blocks.heading: Answer Key
text: **Handout 1 (Test 1)**
**Handout 2**

Present forms: love, do, 's, has, is getting, 's always borrowing, buy, disappears, go, knows, 's constantly singing, has, leaves, is getting, mention, says, see, does, 's having, 'm being, 's cooking, is, tastes, Am I being, Tell.
**Handout 3, Exercise A**
**Handout 3, Exercise B (examples)**
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: is always leaving · 2. is getting · 3. see · 4. are being · 5. starts · 6. always goes · 7. am having · 8. tastes · 9. are ... always interrupting · 10. am seeing

My neighbour is always playing loud music! · 2. You're always interrupting me! · 3. They're always forgetting my name!

The train is leaving at 8 according to the timetable.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute lesson on the historic present for C1 classes, built on the TBL framework, with photocopiable handouts and an answer key.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: Advanced students with a strong command of tenses. They tell stories in the past tense only and are not aware of how and why present forms are used for dramatic effect, live commentary, headlines and summaries.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis to read before you teach, a stage-by-stage procedure with timings and interaction patterns, and the handouts and answer key at the end, ready to print.

items.definition: C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, drop the commentary in Part B and keep the anecdote, then go straight to the analysis.
Speaking, with reading and some writing
Present forms used for past and timeless reference: the historic present in anecdote, live commentary, headlines and plot summary
TBL (Task-Based Learning)

Handout 1 (pre-task headlines), Handout 2 (task instructions and story prompts), Handout 3 (texts for language analysis), Handout 4 (practice), phones for recording (optional), a short silent video clip (sport or cooking, 60–90 seconds) or a set of sequenced images.

About 20 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4 per learner and find a silent video clip of 60 to 90 seconds, or print six images in sequence. Prepare your own one-minute anecdote and decide where you will switch tense.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' ability to recognise and use present forms for dramatic narrative (the historic present), live commentary, newspaper headlines and plot summaries.

**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can tell a short anecdote in the historic present, deliver a 60-second live commentary and write headlines and a plot summary using appropriate present forms.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency and vividness in spoken anecdotes.
**Subsidiary aim.** To raise awareness of genre conventions.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Present continuous for background; present simple for main events
*So I'm walking home and this man comes up to me and says ...*
Present simple for quick completed actions; continuous for longer ones
*He passes to Kumar, Kumar shoots ... and it's in! The crowd is going wild.*
Present simple for past events; *to* + infinitive for future; past participle for passive
*Minister resigns over scandal · President to visit Jaffna · Three injured in crash*
Plot summaries, reviews and reporting what writers argue
*In the novel, the hero returns home ... · Smith argues that ...*
blocks.heading: Uses of present forms with past or general reference
Why use the present?
bullets: It creates **immediacy and drama**: the listener feels the action is happening now.
Speakers often **switch** from past to present at the most exciting moment of a story.
Headlines use the present to save space and to make news feel current.
Summaries use the present because the story "exists" in the text permanently.

blocks.heading: Discourse features of anecdotes
bullets: Fillers and markers: *So ..., Anyway ..., And then ..., Next thing I know ..., Suddenly ...*
Reporting with *says* / *goes* (informal): *And he goes, "Excuse me, is this your bag?"*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: Commentary: fast pace, rising pitch at climaxes, stress on names and key verbs.
Anecdotes: pausing before the key moment for effect.

rows: Students mix tenses randomly rather than for effect.
In analysis, highlight where switches happen and why. Rule of thumb: start in the past, switch to the present for the drama, and stay there.
Students don't see the historic present as "correct" English.
Show authentic-style examples from speech, journalism and literature. Discuss register: very common in speech, less common in formal written narrative.
Over-use of *goes* for *says* in formal contexts.
Point out it is informal speech only.
Weak students struggle to produce commentary in real time.
Let them watch the clip once first and note verbs; allow pairs to share the commentary.
Use a sequence of six images (e.g. a cricket shot or a cooking process) displayed one by one.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: Anecdote · Commentary · Headline · Plot summary · Joke
Background: present continuous (*I'm walking home*) · Events: present simple (*this man comes up*) · Headlines: *resigns / to visit / injured* · Summary: *the hero returns home*
So ... · Anyway ... · And then ... · Next thing I know ... · Suddenly ... · He goes, "..."
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR C1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Historic Present, step by step

stages.name: Pre-task
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic, activate schemata and set up the task.
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Here are six newspaper headlines. With a partner, guess the full story behind each one."* (3 minutes.)
Take some guesses. Ask: *"Did these events happen in the past or are they happening now?"* (Past.) *"So why are the verbs in the present?"* Do not explain yet; say *"We'll come back to that."*

Tell a short anecdote yourself (about 1 minute), switching into the historic present at the dramatic moment. For example: *"Last week I was at the market. It was busy. So I'm standing at the fish stall, and this man comes up behind me and grabs my bag ..."*
Ask: *"Did you notice anything about how I told the story?"* Accept ideas.

**Set the task.** Say: *"Today you're going to be storytellers and commentators. First, tell a partner a true or invented story, and make it as dramatic as possible. Then you will do a live commentary."* Give out Handout 2.

stages.name: Task
stages.time: 15 min · Pairs, then groups of four
text: **Aim:** To give students the opportunity to use language freely for a real communicative purpose.

**Part A, anecdote (7 minutes).** Each student chooses a prompt from Handout 2 (a lost item, a surprise, an embarrassing moment, a near miss). They have one minute to think, then tell their story to a partner in about two minutes. The partner listens and asks two questions.
ICQs: *"How long is your story?"* (About two minutes.) *"What does your partner do?"* (Listens and asks two questions.)

**Part B, commentary (8 minutes).** Play the silent video (or show the images). Say: *"Watch once. Now, in your group of four, take turns to give a 60-second live commentary while the video plays again. Record it on your phone if you can."*
Monitor throughout without correcting. Note language used (or avoided) for later analysis.

stages.name: Planning
text: **Aim:** To give students time to prepare a polished version for the class, focusing on accuracy and impact.
Say: *"Each group chooses the best story and the best commentary. Help the speakers make them even more dramatic and accurate. You will present to the class."*
Groups improve the story and commentary. They may write key sentences. Help with language on request but do not teach the grammar point yet.

stages.name: Report
text: **Aim:** To let groups share their work and to provide a purpose for listening.
Each group presents one story or one commentary (about 1 minute each).
Listening task for the class: *"Which story was the most dramatic? Why?"*
Board two or three sentences you heard that used present forms effectively, and one that did not.
Ask: *"When did the speakers switch to the present? What was the effect?"*

stages.name: Language focus, analysis
text: **Aim:** To raise awareness of the forms and functions of the present in the different genres.
Give out Handout 3 (four extracts: anecdote, commentary, headlines, plot summary). Groups answer the analysis questions (6 minutes).
Feedback as a class. Build the centre of the board: which forms appear in each genre, and why.
Discuss:
Where does the speaker switch from past to present in Extract 1? Why there?
What do the headlines leave out? (Articles, auxiliaries.)
Why is the plot summary in the present?
Highlight the anecdote language (right of the board) and its informal register.

stages.name: Language focus, practice
text: **Aim:** To practise the forms accurately.
Students complete Handout 4, Exercises A and B (6 minutes).
Pairs compare. Check answers as a class.
Exercise C (headline writing): pairs write three headlines for stories told in the lesson and read them out. The class guesses which story each refers to.

blocks.homework: Write a 200-word synopsis of a film or book using the present tense, and three headlines about real events from this week.
blocks.caption: TBL (Task-Based Learning). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Provide the anecdote language as a written list during the task. Let weaker students tell their story first in the past, then retell it in the present with a partner's help.
Stronger students compare the historic present with free indirect speech in a short literary extract. They write a plot summary of a film using the present simple and at least two participle clauses.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Keep the anecdote in pairs and the commentary in fours, both at the same time, and hear only four or five in the Report stage. The analysis works as a whole-class discussion from the board.
Write the six headlines on the board and read the four extracts aloud twice, pausing for learners to note the verb forms. The commentary needs no handout at all once the task is set.
Screen-share the silent clip and mute yourself during the commentary so learners can hear each other. Ask them to record the commentary on their phones and send you one file per group.
With teenagers, use a sports clip and let the commentary be the main task. With adults, add the professional uses of the present: summarising a report, a film or what a writer argues.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students switch to the present deliberately at the climax of their story. The commentary uses the present simple for quick actions and the continuous for longer ones. Students can explain why headlines and summaries use the present. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 4.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did the task generate a natural need for the target language? Did students use the present in the Report stage more effectively than in the first Task? Was the analysis stage long enough?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Headlines
text: **With a partner, guess the full story behind each headline.**
**Think:** Did these events happen in the past, or will they happen in the future? Why do you think the headlines use these verb forms?
bullets: MINISTER RESIGNS OVER SCANDAL
LOCAL GIRL WINS NATIONAL SPELLING BEE
PRESIDENT TO VISIT FLOOD AREA
THREE INJURED IN BUS CRASH NEAR KANDY
ELEPHANT BLOCKS HIGHWAY FOR TWO HOURS
PRICES SET TO RISE AGAIN

blocks.heading: Handout 2: The Task
text: **Part A: Tell a story**
Choose one prompt. Take one minute to think. Then tell your partner your story in about two minutes. Make it dramatic! Your partner listens and asks two questions at the end.
**Part B: Live commentary**
Watch the video once. Then, in your group, take turns to give a 60-second live commentary while the video plays again. Imagine you are on the radio: the listeners cannot see anything!
**Notes**

rows: A time you lost something important (a passport, a phone, a ticket).
A time someone surprised you, or you surprised someone.
A time something embarrassing happened to you in public.
A time something almost went very wrong.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Language Analysis
text: **Extract 1: A spoken anecdote**
**Extract 2: Cricket commentary**
**Extract 3: Headlines**
**Extract 4: Film synopsis**
**Questions**
bullets: In Extract 1, which verbs are in the past? Where does the speaker switch to the present? Why at that moment? ___________________________
Find a present continuous verb in Extract 1. What does it describe: background or main events? ___________________________
In Extract 2, why does the commentator use the present simple for *runs, bowls, pulls*? ___________________________
In Extract 3, what words are missing? What does *to open* mean? Is *stolen* active or passive? ___________________________
Why is Extract 4 in the present simple when the story is fiction and "finished"? ___________________________
Which of these texts is the most informal? Which words show this? ___________________________

blocks.title: The text
text: It was last December, and I was flying home from Dubai. Everything was normal. So I'm sitting there, I'm reading my book, and suddenly the plane drops, like, a hundred metres. People are screaming, drinks are flying everywhere. And the man next to me turns to me, totally calm, and goes, "Is this your first time on a plane?"

And he runs in, he bowls ... it's a short ball, and Perera pulls it ... it's high, it's long, and it's going all the way! That's six! The crowd are on their feet, they're singing, they're dancing in the stands!
STORM HITS COAST: THOUSANDS WITHOUT POWER
NEW BRIDGE TO OPEN IN MAY
PAINTING STOLEN FROM NATIONAL MUSEUM

In the film, a young teacher moves from Colombo to a remote village school. At first, the children ignore her, and the villagers don't trust her. However, when a flood threatens the village, she organises the rescue, and slowly she wins their respect.

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Practice
text: **A. Rewrite the story in the historic present, from the word "So".**
**B. Rewrite each sentence in the style given.**
**C. Write three headlines for stories you heard today.**
bullets: (Headline) The president has visited the flood area. → ___________________________
(Headline) The government will build a new airport. → ___________________________
(Headline) Two people were hurt in a fire. → ___________________________
(Synopsis) In the film, a young girl found a lost dog and looked for its owner. → ___________________________
(Commentary) He hit the ball and it went for six! → ___________________________
(Anecdote) I was walking home when this woman stopped me. → So ___________________________

blocks.title: The text
text: Yesterday I was standing at the bus stop. **So** a car stopped in front of me. The driver opened the window and asked me for directions. I pointed to the left, and he smiled and drove away. Then I realised he had my bag!

blocks.heading: Answer Key
text: **Handout 1:** The headlines use the present simple for past events (1, 2, 4, 5), *to* + infinitive for a future plan (3) and *set to* for a likely future (6). The present makes the news feel current and saves space.
**Handout 3**

**Handout 4, Exercise A (model)** So a car stops in front of me. The driver opens the window and asks me for directions. I point to the left, and he smiles and drives away. Then I realise he has my bag!
**Handout 4, Exercise B**
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: Past: was, was flying, was. The switch happens at *So I'm sitting there*, just before the dramatic event, to make it feel immediate.
*I'm sitting, I'm reading, are screaming, are flying*: background and ongoing actions.
They are quick, completed actions happening as the commentator speaks.
Articles and auxiliaries are missing (*A storm has hit the coast; The new bridge is to open; A painting has been stolen*). *To open* = will open (future plan). *Stolen* = passive.
Plot summaries conventionally use the present because the story exists permanently in the text.
Extract 1: *So, like, totally, goes*.

President visits flood area · 2. Government to build new airport · 3. Two hurt in fire · 4. In the film, a young girl finds a lost dog and looks for its owner. · 5. He hits the ball and it goes for six! · 6. So I'm walking home and this woman stops me.

rows: (Plot summary) At the end, Hamlet died.
Mixing tenses randomly within one scene.
Switch tense once, at the dramatic moment, and stay in the present.
Prime Minister resigns / Prime Minister to resign.
Using *goes* for *says* in a formal essay.
Use *says* or a reporting verb in formal writing.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute lesson on the past simple for A1 classes, built on the PPP framework, with photocopiable handouts and an answer key.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: Beginners who can use the present simple for routines and know common activity verbs. They have heard *was/were* and some past forms but cannot yet form past simple sentences, negatives or questions.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis to read before you teach, a stage-by-stage procedure with timings and interaction patterns, and the handouts and answer key at the end, ready to print.

items.definition: A1 (Beginner)
Teenagers and adults; works with young learners too
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, cut the mingle in Stage 5 to five minutes and set the six written sentences as homework.
Reading and speaking, with some writing
The past simple of be and of regular and irregular verbs, with the -ed endings and did questions and negatives
PPP (Presentation, Practice, Production)
Handout 1 (Sunil's diary), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (Find someone who ...), irregular verb flashcards (go/went, have/had, see/saw, eat/ate, get/got, buy/bought, make/made, do/did).
About 15 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3 per learner and make eight irregular verb flashcards (go/went, have/had, see/saw, eat/ate, get/got, buy/bought, make/made, do/did).

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To present and practise the past simple of *be* and of regular and common irregular verbs to talk about last weekend.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can say and write 6 sentences about their last weekend and ask a classmate *Did you ...?* questions.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To practise the pronunciation of *-ed* endings.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop speaking (asking and answering about past activities).

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: **Was** he happy? Yes, he was. / No, he wasn't.
**Were** you at school? Yes, I was. / No, I wasn't.
blocks.heading: Form: be

rows: We **went** to Galle. He **had** lunch. They **saw** a film.
I **didn't** (did not) **go** out. He **didn't watch** TV.
**Did** you **go** out? Yes, I did. / No, I didn't.
blocks.heading: Form: other verbs (the same for all persons)
Form: other verbs (the same for all persons): notes
text: Spelling of regular verbs:
bullets: Most verbs add *-ed*: play → played, watch → watched.
Verbs ending in *-e* add *-d*: like → liked, dance → danced.
Consonant + *y* → *-ied*: study → studied (but play → played).
One vowel + one consonant: double it: stop → stopped, plan → planned.

blocks.heading: Meaning and use
text: We use the past simple for finished actions at a finished time in the past: *last weekend, yesterday, on Saturday, last night, two days ago*.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation of -ed
bullets: /t/ after voiceless sounds: walked, watched, cooked, danced
/d/ after voiced sounds: played, cleaned, listened, stayed
/ɪd/ after /t/ or /d/: visited, wanted, needed, started

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***I played cricket on Saturday.*** Is Saturday now or in the past? (In the past.) · Is it finished? (Yes.)
***I didn't go out.*** Did I go out? (No.) · After *didn't*, is the verb *go* or *went*? (Go.)

rows: Flashcard drill in the presentation; irregular verb list on Handout 2.
Past form after *didn't* or *did* (*Did you went?*).
Board: did + base verb. Gesture: hold up one finger for "only one past".
Three-column sound sort; drill minimal examples.
Using *was* with other verbs (*I was go*).
Contrast *I was at home* (place/feeling) with *I went home* (action).
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: yesterday · last night · last weekend · on Saturday · two days ago
I **was** at home. They **were** tired. · I play**ed** / **went** / **had**. · I **didn't** go. · **Did** you go? Yes, I did.
/t/ walked, watched · /d/ played, cleaned · /ɪd/ visited, wanted
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults; works with young learners too
blocks.heading: Procedure: Past Simple, step by step

stages.name: Lead-in
text: **Aim:** To engage students and set the context of last weekend.
Write *Saturday* and *Sunday* on the board and draw an arrow pointing backwards. Say: *"Last weekend. Not this weekend. Last weekend."*
Tell the class three things you did, with mime: *"On Saturday, I cleaned my house. I went to the market. On Sunday, I watched a film."*
Ask: *"Did I watch a film?"* (Yes.) *"Did I go to the beach?"* (No.) Students just answer *yes* or *no*.
**Transition:** *"Now read about Sunil's weekend."*

stages.name: Presentation, context
text: **Aim:** To present the language in context.
Give out Handout 1. Say: *"Read Sunil's diary. Tick the things he did. Three minutes."*
ICQs: *"Do you tick things he did or didn't do?"* (Did.)
Students read and tick. Pairs compare. Check answers by asking *"Did Sunil go to the beach?"* and modelling *"Yes, he did."*
Students answer the three comprehension questions.

stages.name: Presentation, language clarification
text: **Aim:** To clarify meaning, form and pronunciation.
**was/were.** Board from the text: *I was very tired. The beach was beautiful. My cousins were there.* Elicit: was for I/he/she/it; were for you/we/they.
**Regular verbs.** Students underline verbs ending in *-ed* in the diary. Board: *visited, played, walked, cooked, watched, stayed*. Elicit the rule: add *-ed*. Show the spelling rules.
**Irregular verbs.** Ask: *"Is there an -ed on went?"* (No.) Board *go → went*. Use flashcards: show the base form; students call out the past form. Repeat quickly three times.
**Negatives.** Board *I didn't go to the cinema.* CCQ: *"Did he go?"* (No.) *"Is it went or go after didn't?"* (Go.)
**Questions.** Board *Did you have a good weekend? Yes, I did.* and *Where did you go?* Highlight did + subject + base verb.
**Pronunciation.** Say *walked, played, visited*. Ask: *"Are the endings the same?"* Draw three columns. Students sort the six verbs from the text. Drill chorally and individually.

stages.name: Practice, controlled
text: **Aim:** To practise the form accurately.
Students complete Handout 2, Exercise A (gap fill) and Exercise B (irregular verbs) alone (6 minutes).
Pairs check. Nominate students to read sentences aloud; correct pronunciation of *-ed* as you go.
**Oral drill:** say a sentence; students make it negative. T: *"I went to the beach."* Ss: *"I didn't go to the beach."* Then: T: *"You / go out?"* Ss: *"Did you go out?"*

stages.name: Production, freer speaking
stages.time: 18 min · Mingle, then whole class, then individual
text: **Aim:** To use the language in a personalised speaking task.
Give out Handout 3. Model the first item with a strong student: *"Did you watch a film last weekend?" "Yes, I did." "What did you watch?"* Write the name in the box.
Say: *"Stand up. Ask your classmates. Find one name for each box. Ask one more question. You have eight minutes."*
ICQs: *"Do you ask one person or many people?"* (Many.) *"What do you write?"* (Names.)
Students mingle. Monitor and note errors with *Did you ...?* and past forms.
Students sit down. Ask several students to report: *"Kasun watched a film. He watched an action film."* (4 minutes.)
**Writing:** students write 6 sentences about their own weekend at the bottom of Handout 3 (4 minutes).

stages.name: Feedback and wrap-up
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Board four sentences from your notes, two correct and two incorrect. Students correct them in pairs.
Quick irregular verb review with the flashcards.
Set homework.

blocks.homework: Write 6 sentences about your last weekend. Include one sentence with *was/were*, two irregular verbs and one negative.
blocks.caption: PPP (Presentation, Practice, Production). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students the verb list with past forms during the mingle. Allow them to answer *Yes, I did / No, I didn't* without follow-up questions.
Stronger students add time phrases (*in the morning, after lunch, at night*). They ask two follow-up questions with *Where? / Who with? / What?*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Replace the Find someone who mingle with a seated version: learners ask the four people nearest them and need only four names, not eight. Drill the irregular verbs chorally by row.

Tell Sunil's weekend as a story twice while learners tick the activities listed on the board. Dictate the practice items. The flashcards can be words written on the board and rubbed out one at a time.
Use the chat for the gap fill so you see every answer. For the mingle, use breakout rooms of three and ask for two names instead of eight; the follow-up question matters more than the number.

With young learners, keep to six regular verbs plus went and had, and make the sound sort a physical one: learners stand for one ending and sit for another. With adults, use last weekend's real plans and allow longer answers.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students use correct past forms in 5 of 6 written sentences. Students form *Did you ...?* questions correctly during the mingle. Students pronounce at least the /ɪd/ endings correctly.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Which irregular verbs caused the most problems? Did the mingle give enough speaking practice for everyone?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Sunil's Diary
text: **Read Sunil's diary. Tick (✓) the things he did last weekend.**
**Answer the questions.**
bullets: Where did Sunil go on Saturday morning? ___________________________
What did he and his cousins do at the beach? ___________________________
What time did he get up on Sunday? ___________________________

blocks.title: The text
text: **Saturday**

In the morning, I visited my grandmother in Galle. We had lunch together: she cooked my favourite fish curry. In the afternoon, my cousins and I went to the beach. The beach was beautiful, and the water was warm. We played volleyball and walked along the beach. I was very tired in the evening, so I stayed at home and watched TV.
**Sunday**

I got up late, at 10 o'clock! I didn't have breakfast. I studied English for two hours, and then I helped my father in the garden. In the evening, my friends wanted to go to the cinema, but I didn't go. I finished my homework and went to bed at 9.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Practice
text: **A. Complete the sentences with the past simple of the verb in brackets.**
**B. Write the past simple form.**
**C. Put the verbs in the correct sound column: walked · played · visited · cooked · cleaned · wanted · watched · stayed · needed**
bullets: I ____________ (visit) my grandmother on Saturday.
We ____________ (go) to the beach.
She ____________ (not / watch) TV.
____________ you ____________ (have) a good weekend?
They ____________ (be) very happy.
My brother ____________ (study) for his exam.
I ____________ (be) tired on Sunday.
We ____________ (not / go) to the cinema.
What ____________ you ____________ (eat) for dinner?

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Find Someone Who ...
text: **Ask your classmates: "Did you ... last weekend?" Write a name. Ask one more question.**
**Now write 6 sentences about your weekend.**

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: Elementary students who use the past simple with reasonable accuracy and know the present continuous. They have not yet learned the past continuous and use the past simple for all past actions.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis to read before you teach, a stage-by-stage procedure with timings and interaction patterns, and the handouts and answer key at the end, ready to print.

items.definition: A2 (Elementary)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, keep the alibi game to one round without swapping roles, and halve the preparation time.
Speaking and reading
The past continuous for actions in progress at a past moment and for actions interrupted by the past simple, with when and while
ESA boomerang (Engage, Activate, Study, Activate)
Handout 1 (news story), Handout 2 (practice), Handout 3 (alibi role cards and detective question sheet).
About 15 minutes: print Handouts 1 and 2 per learner, and one copy of Handout 3 per group of four, cut into the suspects' card and the detectives' sheet.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To clarify and practise the past continuous for actions in progress at a past time and for actions interrupted by a past simple event (*when / while*).
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can say what they were doing at a specific past time and describe an interrupted action, e.g. *I was cooking when the lights went out.*
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in a game-like speaking task (an alibi game).
**Subsidiary aim.** To read a short news story for specific information.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: **Was** she work**ing**? Yes, she was. / No, she wasn't.
**Were** you study**ing**? Yes, I was. / No, I wasn't.
blocks.heading: Form
Meaning and use
bullets: An action **in progress at a specific time** in the past: *At 8 pm last night, I was watching TV.*
A **longer action interrupted** by a shorter one: *I was walking home when it started to rain.* (past continuous = long action; past simple = short action)
**when** usually goes before the short action; **while** usually goes before the long action: *While she was sleeping, the phone rang.*
Two actions in progress at the same time: *While I was cooking, my brother was doing his homework.*

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *was* and *were* are usually weak in positive sentences: /wəz/, /wə/. *I was cooking* /aɪ wəz ˈkʊkɪŋ/.
They are strong in short answers and negatives: *Yes, I was* /wɒz/. *wasn't* /ˈwɒznt/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***I was cooking when the lights went out.*** Which action started first? (Cooking.) · Which action was short? (The lights went out.) · Did the lights going out interrupt the cooking? (Yes.) · Which is in the past continuous? (Cooking.)

rows: Board formula with three boxes. Finger gesture: three fingers for *was – watch – ing*.
Using the continuous for both actions (*When I was arriving, they were eating*).
Timeline: one long wavy line, one cross. CCQ: *Which is short?*
Highlight the general pattern on the board; accept *when* with both in speech.
Alibi game: students forget their story.
Give each pair time to write a short alibi plan on the card.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: the lights went out · the phone rang · it started to rain · power cut · alibi · suspect

Timeline: ~~~~~ (long action) interrupted by X (short action). I **was cooking** when the lights **went** out. While she **was sleeping**, the phone **rang**. was/were + verb-ing. Q: What **were** you **doing** at 8?
I was cooking /wəz/ · They were watching /wə/ · Yes, I was /wɒz/
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR A2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Past Continuous, step by step

stages.name: Engage
text: **Aim:** To generate interest and get students talking about a past moment.
Turn off the classroom lights (or mime it). Say: *"Imagine: last night at 8 o'clock, all the lights in the city went out! A power cut!"*
Ask: *"Do you remember a power cut? Where were you? How did you feel?"* Take two or three answers.
Write *7 o'clock this morning* on the board. Students tell a partner what they did this morning (1 minute). Listen; don't correct.

stages.name: Activate 1, first try
text: **Aim:** To let students try a communicative task with the language they have, and to diagnose needs.

Say: *"Last night at 8 pm, there was a power cut in our town. Ask your partner: what was your family doing at that moment? Imagine if you don't remember! Find out about four people in your partner's family."* (4 minutes.)
Monitor without helping. Note: (a) whether students use the past continuous; (b) errors; (c) any good examples.
Ask two or three pairs to report one thing. Say: *"Great. Let's read about the real power cut."*

stages.name: Study, reading and language focus
text: **Aim:** To clarify the meaning, form and pronunciation of the past continuous with *when / while*.
Give out Handout 1. **Reading task:** *"Read the news story. Match each person to what they were doing when the lights went out."* (3 minutes.) Pairs check, then class feedback.
**Noticing:** students underline *was/were + -ing* verbs in one colour and past simple verbs in another.
**Meaning.** Board *Mr Perera was cooking when the lights went out.* Draw a timeline. Ask the CCQs.
**Form.** Elicit the form table: was/were + verb-ing; negative; question. Board: *What were you doing at 8 pm?*
**when / while.** Board two sentences from the text with *when* and *while*. Ask: *"Which word comes before the long action?"* (while). *"Which comes before the short action?"* (when).
**Pronunciation.** Drill with weak forms: *I was cooking. They were watching TV.* Then strong short answers: *Yes, I was.*
**Activate 1 errors.** Board two or three sentences you heard in Activate 1. Pairs improve them using today's language.

stages.name: Study, controlled practice
text: **Aim:** To practise the form and the contrast with the past simple.
Students complete Handout 2, Exercises A and B (6 minutes).
Pairs compare and justify: *"It's the long action, so past continuous."*
Check as a class. Drill two or three of the sentences.

stages.name: Activate 2, the alibi game
stages.time: 17 min · Groups of four (two suspects, two detectives)
text: **Aim:** To use the language fluently and accurately in a communicative game, repeating the Activate 1 skill at a higher level.
**Set up.** Read the situation on Handout 3: *"Yesterday between 10.00 and 11.00, a birthday cake disappeared from the staff room. Two students are suspects."*
Divide each group: two suspects (Pair S) and two detectives (Pair D). Suspects get the alibi card; detectives get the question sheet.

**Preparation (4 minutes).** Suspects agree on a detailed alibi: where they were, what they were doing at 10.00, 10.15, 10.30 and 10.45, who they saw. Detectives prepare questions using the question sheet.
**Interviews (6 minutes).** Detectives interview each suspect **separately** (the other suspect waits out of earshot). Detectives note answers.

**Decision (2 minutes).** Detectives compare notes: are there differences? They decide: *innocent* or *guilty*, and give reasons: *"Suspect A said they were reading in the library at 10.30, but Suspect B said they were eating in the canteen."*
If time allows, swap roles and play again.

stages.name: Feedback
text: **Aim:** To consolidate and correct.
Each group announces its verdict with one reason.
Board four sentences from the game: two correct, two with errors. Students correct them.
Ask: *"Was Activate 2 easier than Activate 1? Why?"*
Set homework.

blocks.homework: Write a paragraph (80–100 words) about where you were and what you were doing during a memorable event (a big match, a storm, a celebration).
blocks.caption: ESA boomerang (Engage, Activate, Study, Activate). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give suspects a time-plan template to complete before the interviews. Weaker detectives can read questions directly from the sheet.

Detectives must ask at least two follow-up questions (*Exactly what time? Who were you with? What were they wearing?*). Stronger suspects add a while sentence: *While I was reading, Kamal was sitting next to me.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Run the alibi game in groups of four at their desks, all at once, and hear only four verdicts. Keep the suspects in the room but seat the second suspect facing away while the first is questioned.

Read the power cut report aloud twice while learners match the four people to four activities written on the board. The alibi game needs only the time plan, which learners can rule up in their own books.
Send the second suspect to a waiting room while the first is interviewed, which makes the game work better online than in a classroom. Put the detectives' questions in the chat.

With young learners, make the missing object a classroom one and keep the interview to three questions. With adults, add the follow-up questions about clothing and other people, which is where the contradictions appear.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: In Activate 2, students form past continuous questions and answers accurately most of the time. Students choose past continuous vs past simple correctly in 8 of 10 items on Handout 2. Students use *when* and *while* in at least one sentence each.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: How much did students improve from Activate 1 to Activate 2? Was the alibi game well organised? How could I set it up faster?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Power Cut!
text: **Read the news story. Match each person to what they were doing when the lights went out.**
**True or false?**
bullets: The power cut lasted for one hour. ______
Nimali saved her essay. ______
Mrs Fernando was worried. ______

blocks.title: The text
text: **CITY IN THE DARK**
At exactly 8 pm last night, all the lights in the city went out. The power cut lasted for two hours. We asked some people what they were doing.
"I was cooking dinner for my family," said Mr Perera, 45. "The rice was nearly ready. We ate by candlelight!"
Nimali, 16, was doing her homework when the lights went out. "I was writing an essay on my computer. I didn't save it, so I lost everything!"
While the city was sitting in the dark, two doctors at the General Hospital were working with torches. "We were helping a patient, and we didn't stop," said Dr Silva.
Mrs Fernando, 70, wasn't worried. "I was sleeping in my chair. I didn't notice anything!"

**B. Choose when or while.**
**C. Answer about you. What were you doing ...**
