hero.text: A complete 60-minute lesson on the past perfect for B1 classes, built on the Guided Discovery framework, with photocopiable handouts and an answer key.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: Intermediate students who use the past simple and past continuous but rarely use the past perfect, so their stories are hard to follow when events are not told in order.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis to read before you teach, a stage-by-stage procedure with timings and interaction patterns, and the handouts and answer key at the end, ready to print.

items.definition: B1 (Intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, put learners in pairs rather than threes for the storytelling and hear two stories.
Speaking and reading, with some writing
The past perfect alongside the past simple and past continuous in narrative, with sequencing words and the contracted 'd
Guided Discovery
Handout 1 (story strips, cut up), Handout 2 (discovery task), Handout 3 (practice), Handout 4 (story prompt cards and listener sheet).
About 20 minutes: cut up one set of story strips (Handout 1) per pair, and print Handouts 2 to 4 per learner. Prepare the first two sentences of a story of your own that uses all three tenses.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To help students discover and use the past simple, past continuous and past perfect together to tell a clear personal story.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can tell a two-minute personal story using all three narrative tenses and at least four sequencers.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To practise sequencing words.
**Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in storytelling.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise contracted *'d*.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: I realised I **had left** my passport at home.
blocks.heading: Form and use
Form and use: notes
text: Sequencers: *at first, then, after that, suddenly, as soon as, by the time, eventually, in the end*.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *had* is usually contracted in speech: *I'd left* /aɪd left/, *she'd gone*. Students often don't hear the *'d*.
Weak *had* in full form: /əd/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***When I got to the gate, the plane had left.*** Which happened first: I got to the gate, or the plane left? (The plane left.) · Did I see the plane leave? (No.) · Which tense shows the earlier action? (Past perfect.)
***It was raining when I left home.*** Did the rain start before I left? (Yes.) · Is it a main event in the story or the background? (Background.)

rows: Not using the past perfect (*When I arrived, the plane left* = it left as I arrived).
Contrast the two meanings with timelines; CCQs.
Emphasise: only for the earlier event, when the order is not clear.
Give prompt questions on the story cards; listeners must ask two follow-up questions.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: at first · then · after that · suddenly · as soon as · by the time · eventually · in the end
Timeline: [had left passport] → [was raining / arrived at airport] → [realised]. Background = past continuous · Main events = past simple · Earlier = past perfect (had + pp)
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Past Perfect, step by step

stages.name: Lead-in
text: **Aim:** To engage interest and personalise the topic.
Ask: *"Have you ever had a problem on a journey? Missed a bus, lost a ticket?"* Give your own one-sentence example.
Students share with a partner in one or two sentences (2 minutes).
Take two examples from the class.

stages.name: Context, story strips
text: **Aim:** To present the target language in a story context.
Give each pair the cut-up story strips (Handout 1). Say: *"This is a story called The Day I Missed My Flight. Put the strips in order. Look for clues in the verbs and sequencing words."* (4 minutes.)
Pairs compare with another pair. Read the story aloud in the correct order for students to check.
Gist question: *"Did the story have a happy ending?"*

stages.name: Discovery task
text: **Aim:** To guide students to work out the uses of the three tenses.
Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Look at the four sentences from the story. Answer the questions with your partner."*
Monitor. Help struggling pairs by asking: *"Which happened first? Draw it."*
Pairs draw timelines for sentences 3 and 4.
Pairs compare with another pair.

stages.name: Check and clarify
text: **Aim:** To confirm rules and clarify form and pronunciation.
Elicit the answers to the discovery questions. Build the timeline and rules on the board.
Ask the CCQs from the Language analysis.
**Meaning contrast:** board *When I got to the gate, the plane left* vs *When I got to the gate, the plane had left.* Ask: *"In which sentence did I see the plane leave?"* (The first.)
**Form:** had + past participle; contraction 'd. Elicit three irregular participles (left, forgotten, gone).
**Pronunciation:** drill *I'd left my passport at home*, slowly and then at natural speed.

stages.name: Controlled practice
text: **Aim:** To practise choosing and forming the tenses accurately.
Students complete Handout 3, Exercise A (story gap fill) and Exercise B (join the sentences) (6 minutes).
Pairs compare. Check as a class and ask for timeline explanations for two items.

stages.name: Freer practice, storytelling
text: **Aim:** To use narrative tenses fluently in personal stories.
Give each group a set of prompt cards (Handout 4). Each student chooses one card and plans a story for 2 minutes, making notes (not full sentences).
Model briefly: tell the first two sentences of your own story using all three tenses.
Students take turns to tell their stories (about 2 minutes each). Listeners complete the listener sheet: tick each tense they hear and write one follow-up question.
After each story, listeners ask their follow-up questions.
Monitor and note errors and good examples.

stages.name: Feedback
text: **Aim:** To give feedback and consolidate.
Each group nominates the best story; one or two are retold briefly to the class.
Board errors and good sentences from your notes for students to correct and notice.
Set homework.

blocks.homework: Write a 150-word story that begins: *It was a perfectly normal day until ...*
blocks.caption: Guided Discovery. Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker students a story skeleton: *It was ... (background). I was ... when ... . I realised I had ... . In the end, ...* Allow them to write their story notes in more detail.
Stronger students add feelings with adjectives and adverbs (*terrified, luckily, unfortunately*). They try the past perfect continuous: *I had been waiting for an hour.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: One set of strips per four learners rather than per pair. Keep the storytelling in threes and hear two stories in open class; the listener sheet keeps everyone else accountable.
Write the eight story strips on the board out of order and have learners number them in their books. The story prompts can be read aloud; the listener sheet is three columns learners draw themselves.
Put the strips in a shared document for pairs to drag into order. Breakout rooms of three for the storytelling, with the listener sheet pasted into each room's chat.
With young learners, use a lost toy and keep the story to four sentences. With adults, a journey or a first day at work gives the past perfect something real to do.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Students use the past perfect correctly at least once in their story. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 3. Listeners can identify all three tenses in a partner's story.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did the story strips work as a context? Could students explain the past perfect in their own words?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Story Strips (cut up)
text: **The Day I Missed My Flight**

rows: **A.** I ran to the check-in desk. People were queuing everywhere and everyone was rushing.
**B.** Last December, I was flying to Dubai for my cousin's wedding. I was very excited.
**C.** I called my brother. He jumped in a tuk-tuk and brought it to me, but when I got to the gate, the plane had left.
**D.** By the time I arrived at the airport, it was already 6.30. My flight was at 7.
**E.** In the end, I arrived in Dubai six hours late, but I didn't miss the wedding!
**F.** On the morning of the flight, it was raining heavily and the roads were full of traffic.
**G.** When I got to the desk, I opened my bag and realised that I had left my passport at home!
**H.** I was so upset. But then a kind airline worker found me a seat on the next flight.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: Discovery Task
text: **Look at these sentences from the story.**
**Answer the questions with your partner.**
bullets: It **was raining** heavily and the roads **were** full of traffic.
I **ran** to the check-in desk.
I **realised** that I **had left** my passport at home.
When I **got** to the gate, the plane **had left**.
In sentence 1, is the rain a main event in the story, or is it the background (the scene)? ___________________________
In sentence 2, is running a main event? ___________________________
In sentence 3, which happened first: *realised* or *left my passport*? ___________________________
Draw a timeline for sentence 3.
In sentence 4, did the writer see the plane leave? ___________________________
What is the form of the verb for the earlier action? ______ + ___________________________
Complete the rules:
We use the ____________________ for the main events of a story.
We use the ____________________ for the background.
We use the ____________________ for an action that happened before another past action.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Practice
text: **A. Complete the story with the correct narrative tense.**

When I (1) ____________ (arrive) at the station, the train (2) ____________ (already / leave). It (3) ____________ (rain) and everyone (4) ____________ (run) for shelter. I (5) ____________ (realise) that I (6) ____________ (forget) my umbrella. While I (7) ____________ (wait) for the next train, I (8) ____________ (meet) an old school friend. In the end, we (9) ____________ (catch) the next train together and (10) ____________ (talk) all the way home.
**B. Join the sentences using the word in brackets. Use the past perfect for the earlier action.**
bullets: The film started. Then we arrived at the cinema. (When) → ___________________________
I finished my homework. Then I went out. (after) → ___________________________
She lost her keys. She couldn't get into the house. (because) → ___________________________
They didn't eat all day. They were very hungry. (because) → ___________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Story Cards and Listener Sheet
text: **Listener sheet:** tick the tenses you hear and write a follow-up question.

rows: **A lost item** When was it? Where were you? What were you doing? When did you realise? What had happened?
**A big surprise** Who surprised you? What were you doing? What had they planned?
**An embarrassing moment** Where were you? Who was there? What happened? Had you prepared for it?
**A journey that went wrong** Where were you going? What was the weather like? What had you forgotten?

text: **Handout 1 (correct order):** B, F, D, A, G, C, H, E
**Handout 2**
**Handout 3, Exercise A**
**Handout 3, Exercise B**
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: Background · 2. Yes, a main event · 3. Left my passport happened first · 5. No · 6. had + past participle · 7. past simple; past continuous; past perfect
arrived · 2. had already left · 3. was raining · 4. was running · 5. realised · 6. had forgotten · 7. was waiting · 8. met · 9. caught · 10. talked

When we arrived at the cinema, the film had started. · 2. I went out after I had finished my homework. · 3. She couldn't get into the house because she had lost her keys. · 4. They were very hungry because they hadn't eaten all day.

rows: When I arrived, the film already started.
When I arrived, the film had already started.
I was knowing him for years.
I had known him for years.

hero.text: A complete 60-minute lesson on the past perfect continuous for B2 classes, built on the TTT framework, with photocopiable handouts and an answer key.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: Upper-intermediate students who know the past perfect simple but rarely use the past perfect continuous, and confuse the two when talking about causes and duration.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis to read before you teach, a stage-by-stage procedure with timings and interaction patterns, and the handouts and answer key at the end, ready to print.

items.definition: B2 (Upper-intermediate)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, let groups explain their scene aloud instead of writing it, and hear two groups.
Speaking and reading, with some writing
The past perfect continuous against the past perfect simple: duration and visible evidence against a completed result, and the stative verbs that stay simple
TTT (Test, Teach, Test)
Handout 1 (Test 1), Handout 2 (detective's notes), Handout 3 (language reference and practice), Handout 4 (scene cards for Test 2).
About 15 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 3 per learner and one scene card (Handout 4) per group of four. Read Test 1 first so you can note problem items while monitoring.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To diagnose and improve students' use of the past perfect simple and continuous to explain causes, visible results and duration before a past moment.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can explain a past scene logically, e.g. *The floor was wet because it had been raining and someone had left the window open.*
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop fluency in speculating and explaining.
**Subsidiary aim.** To practise weak forms of *had been*.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: Completed action before a past moment (result, number)
By 10 pm, he **had written** three emails.
Activity continuing up to a past moment (duration)
She **had been working** there for ten years when she resigned.
Visible result of a recent activity
His eyes were red because he **had been crying**.
I **had known** him for years. (not *had been knowing*)
blocks.heading: Meaning and use
Meaning and use: notes
text: Time markers: *by the time, by (10 pm), for, since, already, just, when, before*.

blocks.heading: Pronunciation
bullets: *had been* is weak and contracted: *She'd been working* /ʃid bɪn ˈwɜːkɪŋ/.

blocks.heading: Concept-checking questions
bullets: ***The ground was wet. It had been raining.*** Was it raining at the moment I looked? (Not necessarily; maybe it had stopped.) · Was the rain before the moment I saw the ground? (Yes.) · Can we see a result? (Yes, the wet ground.)
***By the time I arrived, they had finished the meeting.*** Was the meeting finished when I arrived? (Yes.) · Is the focus on the activity or the completion? (Completion.)

rows: State verbs in the continuous (*had been knowing*).
Mini state verb list on the board.
Continuous with a number of things (*had been writing three emails*).
Using past simple instead (*He was tired because he ran*).
Accept as possible in some cases; show that the past perfect makes the order clear.
Provide clue prompts on the scene cards.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: Simple: had + pp → completed result / number: had written three emails · Continuous: had been + -ing → duration / activity / visible evidence: had been raining · State verbs → simple only: had known
She'd been working /ʃid bɪn/ · had been /əd bɪn/
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR B2 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Past Perfect Continuous, step by step

stages.name: Lead-in
text: **Aim:** To engage interest with a visual puzzle.
Describe or show a photo: *A man arrives at the office. He's soaking wet, exhausted, his shoes are muddy and he's holding a broken umbrella.*
Ask: *"Why? What had happened to him before he arrived?"* Students speculate with a partner (2 minutes). Don't correct.
Take a few ideas.

stages.name: Test 1
text: **Aim:** To diagnose students' current knowledge.
Say: *"This is a test for me, not for you: I want to know what you need. Work alone. Seven minutes."* Give out Handout 1.
Monitor and record which items many students get wrong.

stages.name: Diagnose
text: **Aim:** To identify the main problem areas.
Pairs compare answers and discuss differences.
Poll the class on each item (*"Who has had finished? Who has had been finishing?"*). Do not confirm.
Board the item numbers that caused most disagreement.

stages.name: Teach
text: **Aim:** To clarify the problem areas identified.
**Context.** Give out Handout 2 (detective's notes). Say: *"Read the detective's notes. What had the suspect been doing before 10 pm?"* (3 minutes.) Check answers.
**Noticing.** Students underline all past perfect forms and sort them into simple and continuous.
**Clarify.** Draw timelines for one example of each. Ask the CCQs. Focus especially on the items from the Diagnose stage.
Elicit the rules: result / number → simple; duration / activity / evidence → continuous; state verbs → simple.
**Pronunciation.** Drill weak forms: *She'd been working. They'd been waiting for hours.*
Students do Handout 3, Exercise A (4 minutes), and check in pairs.
Give the answers to Test 1. Students mark their own work.

stages.name: Test 2, deduction game
stages.time: 20 min · Pairs, then groups of four, then whole class
text: **Aim:** To check improvement through a freer speaking and writing task.
Pairs correct their Test 1 answers (3 minutes).

Give each group a scene card (Handout 4). Say: *"You are detectives. Look at the clues. Explain exactly what had happened and what people had been doing before the police arrived. Write your explanation: at least six sentences using both past perfect forms."* (10 minutes.)
ICQs: *"How many sentences?"* (At least six.) *"Which forms?"* (Both past perfect forms.)
Monitor and help with logic and language.
Groups present their explanation (1 minute each). Other groups challenge: *"But if he had been sleeping, why was the coffee hot?"*
Class votes for the most convincing explanation.

stages.name: Feedback
text: **Aim:** To compare Test 1 and Test 2 and give feedback.
Board sentences heard during the presentations: correct and incorrect. Students correct them.
Ask: *"What do you understand now that you didn't understand in Test 1?"*
Set homework.

blocks.homework: Write the detective's final report (180 words) explaining what had happened in your group's scene.
blocks.caption: TTT (Test, Teach, Test). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give weaker groups the timeline images on their scene cards. Provide sentence starters: *The window was open because someone had ... . The floor was wet because ... had been ...*
Stronger groups include passive forms: *The window had been forced.* They use modal deductions: *He must have been sleeping.*

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Poll Test 1 by show of hands and board only the two or three items that split the class. Give each group of four one scene and hear four explanations, not all of them.
Dictate the eight Test 1 items. Read the detective's notes aloud twice while learners listen for what the suspect had been doing. Describe one scene aloud for the whole class to explain together.

Test 1 by private message. Breakout rooms of four for the deduction task with one scene pasted into each room, then let groups challenge each other's explanations in the main room, which works well on screen.
With teenagers, use the school office scene and keep it light. With adults, the bus station and the villa produce longer explanations; invite them to add a passive form, which comes naturally here.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: Fewer errors in Test 2 than in Test 1 on the simple / continuous distinction. Correct use of state verbs in the simple form. 7 out of 8 or better on Handout 3, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did Test 1 identify the right problems? Was the deduction game motivating?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Test 1
text: **Complete with the past perfect simple or the past perfect continuous of the verb in brackets.**
bullets: The ground was wet. It ____________________ (rain) all night.
By the time I arrived, they ____________________ (finish) the meeting.
She was tired because she ____________________ (study) since dawn.
I ____________________ (know) him for years before we became friends.
They ____________________ (wait) for two hours when the bus finally came.
By midnight, he ____________________ (write) four chapters of his book.
How long ____________ you ____________________ (live) there before you moved?
Her hands were covered in paint. She ____________________ (decorate) her room.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: The Detective's Notebook
text: **Questions**
bullets: What had the suspect been doing before 10 pm? How do we know? ___________________________
What had someone done to the lock? ___________________________
Why don't the detectives believe his story about the film? ___________________________

blocks.title: The text
text: **Detective Jayasinghe, 11 March, 10.15 pm**

When we arrived at the flat at 10 pm, the door was open. Someone had forced the lock. The suspect, Mr Dias, was sitting on the sofa. He was breathing heavily, and his shirt was wet: he had obviously been running.

The kitchen was a mess. Someone had been cooking: there was rice on the floor, and the cooker was still warm. Two glasses were on the table. Mr Dias said he had been watching a film all evening, but the TV was cold. He hadn't been watching anything.
His neighbour told us she had heard shouting at about 9.30. She had been living next door for five years and had never heard anything like it before.
By the end of the interview, Mr Dias had changed his story three times.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Language Focus and Practice
text: **Language reference**
**A. Choose the correct form.**
**B. Write an explanation for each situation using the past perfect continuous.**
bullets: When I got home, my sister **had cooked / had been cooking** dinner, so we ate immediately.
Her eyes were red. She **had cried / had been crying**.
We **had walked / had been walking** for hours when we found the village.
By 2015, he **had visited / had been visiting** twelve countries.
I **had known / had been knowing** her since primary school.
The children were dirty because they **had played / had been playing** in the garden.
She **had read / had been reading** the book twice before the film came out.
How long **had you waited / had you been waiting** when the doctor arrived?
The teacher's voice was very tired. → ___________________________
The streets were full of water. → ___________________________

rows: Completed action / result: *Someone had forced the lock.*
Activity up to a past moment: *He had been running.*
Number or quantity: *He had changed his story three times.*
Duration: *She had been living there for five years.*
State verbs: *I had known him for years.*
Visible evidence: *His shirt was wet; he had been running.*

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Scene Cards (Test 2)
text: **Scene 1: The holiday villa** Police arrive at 11 am. The front door is locked. A back window is open. The swimming pool area is wet. There are two towels on chairs. A cake is half eaten. The guest's car is gone. A phone on the table shows 14 missed calls.

**Scene 2: The school office** The principal arrives at 7 am. Papers are all over the floor. The computer is on and warm. There's a cup of coffee, still hot. The cleaner is sitting outside, looking nervous. Exam papers are missing.

**Scene 3: The wedding hall** The guests arrive at 6 pm. The bride is crying. The decorations are only half finished. There are flowers on the floor. The cake has fallen over. The DJ is asleep behind his equipment.
**Scene 4: The bus station** At 9 pm, a bus arrives three hours late. The passengers look exhausted and angry. The bus is covered in mud. One tyre is new. The driver's clothes are wet.
**Write your group's explanation here (at least 6 sentences):**

pages.title: Inversion and Participle Clauses ESL Lesson Plan (C1, 60 Minutes)
pages.metaTitle: Inversion and Participle Clauses ESL Lesson Plan (C1)
pages.description: Free 60-minute C1 ESL lesson plan on the inversion and participle clauses: aims, language analysis, timed stages, printable handouts and a full answer key.
pages.keywords: inversion and participle clauses lesson plan, inversion and participle clauses ESL lesson, teaching the inversion and participle clauses, C1 ESL lesson plan, TBL lesson plan, free ESL lesson plans
pages.teaches: Past Perfect in Inversion and Participle Clauses (No sooner had ... / Having + past participle) (English grammar)

hero.text: A complete 60-minute lesson on the inversion and participle clauses for C1 classes, built on the TBL framework, with photocopiable handouts and an answer key.

blocks.heading: About this lesson
text: Advanced students who write accurate but "flat" narratives in which every sentence has the same structure. They have met negative inversion but rarely use it.

Everything the lesson needs is on this page: the language analysis to read before you teach, a stage-by-stage procedure with timings and interaction patterns, and the handouts and answer key at the end, ready to print.

items.definition: C1 (Advanced)
Teenagers and adults
60 minutes. For 45 minutes, skip the swap-and-compare step in the Task and have two pairs read in the Report stage.
Writing and speaking
Delaying structures, negative inversion with no sooner, hardly and never, was about to, and participle clauses, used to build suspense in narrative
TBL (Task-Based Learning)
Handout 1 (two openings), Handout 2 (task: the flat paragraph), Handout 3 (analysis), Handout 4 (practice and style checklist).
About 15 minutes: print Handouts 1 to 4 per learner. Read both openings aloud once beforehand so the contrast lands in the Pre-task stage.

blocks.heading: Aims
text: **Main aim.** To develop students' ability to create suspense in written narrative using delaying structures, negative inversion, *was about to / was going to*, and participle clauses.
**Learning outcome.** By the end of the lesson, students can rewrite a flat paragraph into a suspenseful one using at least four techniques, and explain the effect of each.
bullets: **Subsidiary aim.** To develop collaborative writing and peer-editing skills.
**Subsidiary aim.** To raise awareness of sentence rhythm.

blocks.heading: Language analysis
text: What to know before the lesson: the meaning, form and pronunciation of the target language, and the problems learners usually have with it.

rows: I **was just reaching** for the door **when** the light went out.
*No sooner had + S + pp ... than*; *Hardly / Scarcely / Barely had + S + pp ... when*
**No sooner had I sat down than** the phone rang. **Hardly had** she left **when** the storm began.
Inversion with *Never / Not until / Only then*
**Never had I felt** so alone. **Only then did I realise** the truth.
*was about to / was going to* + infinitive
I **was about to** scream **when** a hand covered my mouth.
**Having locked** the door, she turned off the lights. **Hearing** a noise, he froze.
long sentence followed by a very short one
... and I walked slowly down the corridor, counting the doors, listening for any sound. **Silence.**
blocks.heading: Techniques
Accuracy points
bullets: *No sooner* ... **than** (not *when*); *Hardly / Scarcely* ... **when** (not *than*).
The participle clause must share the subject of the main clause (avoid dangling participles: *Having locked the door, the lights went out* ✗).

blocks.heading: Pronunciation (when reading aloud)
bullets: Pause before the key event; lower volume for tension; stress the inverted auxiliary: *No sooner HAD I ...*

rows: Wrong word order after inversion (*No sooner I had arrived*).
Show the "question order" pattern; quick transformation drill.
Board the pairs clearly and include in practice.
Include one deliberate example in the analysis for students to spot.
Overuse of techniques making writing heavy.
Discuss balance in feedback; checklist limits each technique to once or twice.
blocks.heading: Anticipated problems and solutions

rows: delaying · inversion · about to · participle clauses · short sentences
No sooner **had I** + pp **than** ... · Hardly **had she** + pp **when** ... · Never **had I** felt ... · I **was about to** ... **when** ... · **Having** + pp, S + V
blocks.heading: Board plan

blocks.eyebrow: CEFR C1 · 60 minutes · Teenagers and adults
blocks.heading: Procedure: Inversion and Participle Clauses, step by step

stages.name: Pre-task
text: **Aim:** To introduce the topic of suspense and set up the task.
Read aloud two openings from Handout 1 (Version A: flat; Version B: suspenseful). Ask: *"Which one would you continue reading? Why?"*
Pairs discuss what makes Version B more exciting (2 minutes). Take ideas but do not name the grammar yet.

**Set the task.** Give out Handout 2. Say: *"Your task is to rewrite this flat paragraph so that it is full of suspense. Then you'll read it aloud to the class and we'll vote for the most gripping version. Work in pairs."*

stages.name: Task
text: **Aim:** To give students a meaningful writing task in which they use their existing language.
Pairs rewrite the paragraph (10 minutes). They may add details, change the order and change sentence lengths, but the basic events must stay the same.
Monitor without correcting. Note structures students use or avoid.
After 10 minutes, pairs swap with another pair and read each other's versions (3 minutes). Each pair underlines the line they think is most effective.

stages.name: Planning
text: **Aim:** To prepare for public performance and improve the text.
Say: *"You will read your version to the class. Improve it using your partners' feedback. Practise reading it aloud: where will you pause?"*
Help with language on request.

stages.name: Report
text: **Aim:** To share the outcomes and provide a reason to listen.
Four or five pairs read their versions aloud (about 1 minute each).
Listeners note the line they find most suspenseful.
Class votes for the most gripping version.
Board two or three of the most effective lines heard.

stages.name: Language focus, analysis
text: **Aim:** To raise awareness of the structures professional writers use to create suspense.
Give out Handout 3. Groups compare Version A and Version B from Handout 1 and complete the analysis table: for each change, name the technique and describe the effect (6 minutes).
Class feedback. Build the centre of the board with the patterns.
Focus on accuracy: *No sooner ... than* vs *Hardly ... when*; word order after inversion; the dangling participle in Question 4.
Ask: *"Which of these techniques did you already use in your task? Which did nobody use?"*

stages.name: Language focus, practice
text: **Aim:** To practise the structures accurately.
Students complete Handout 4, Exercise A (transformations) (5 minutes). Pairs check. Feedback.
**Exercise B:** pairs improve two sentences from their own task using a technique they hadn't used, then check against the style checklist.

blocks.homework: Write a 250-word suspense story opening. Use the style checklist and highlight each technique you use.
blocks.caption: TBL (Task-Based Learning). Stage times add up to 60 minutes.

items.definition: Give model sentences for each technique on a reference card. Pair weaker students with stronger writers for the task.
Students vary the point of view or use free indirect speech. They write the next paragraph of the story for homework, using a technique not yet practised.

blocks.heading: Adapting the lesson
rows: Pairs rewrite as normal, then four or five read aloud rather than all. The swap-and-underline step in Stage 2 gives every pair a reader without taking class time.
Read both openings aloud and dictate the flat paragraph; it is eight short sentences. Board the five techniques as patterns and let learners copy them, which they will need for the rewrite anyway.
Pairs write in a shared document so you can watch drafts appear and prompt a technique nobody has used. Reading aloud over audio suits this lesson: ask for the pause before the key event.
With teenagers, a school or a night bus works better than a house. With adults, keep the original paragraph but ask for a genre: crime, ghost story or thriller, which changes the detail they choose.

blocks.heading: Checking learning
text: The final text uses at least four techniques accurately. Students can name and explain each technique. 8 out of 10 or better on Handout 4, Exercise A.

blocks.heading: Teacher's reflection
text: Did the task produce interesting writing before the language focus? Did the language focus help students improve the second draft?

blocks.heading: Handout 1: Two Openings
text: **Version A**
**Version B**
**Discuss:** Which version do you want to continue reading? Why?

blocks.title: The text
text: I got home at 11 pm. I opened the door. The house was dark. I turned on the light, but it didn't work. I heard a noise upstairs. I went up the stairs. A door was open. I looked inside. There was nobody there. Then the phone rang.

It was almost midnight by the time I reached the house. Having fumbled for my keys in the dark, I pushed the door open and reached for the light switch. Nothing. I was about to call out when I heard it: a slow, heavy footstep, directly above my head. Never had the staircase seemed so long. I was halfway up, counting each step, holding my breath, when I noticed that my bedroom door, the door I always close, was wide open. I stepped inside. Empty. No sooner had I let out a breath than the phone began to ring.

blocks.heading: Handout 2: The Task
text: **Rewrite this paragraph so that it is full of suspense. Keep the same basic events.**
**Your version:**

blocks.title: The text
text: Maya was walking home from the station. It was late and the street was empty. She heard footsteps behind her. She walked faster. The footsteps got faster too. She turned the corner and saw her house. She ran to the door. She couldn't find her key. A hand touched her shoulder. It was her brother.

blocks.heading: Handout 3: Analysis
text: **Compare Version A and Version B. Find an example of each technique and describe its effect.**
**Think about accuracy.**
bullets: What is the word order after *No sooner*? ___________________________
Which word follows *No sooner*: *than* or *when*? ___________________________
Which word follows *Hardly*: *than* or *when*? ___________________________
What is wrong with this sentence? *Having locked the door, the lights went out.* ___________________________

blocks.heading: Handout 4: Practice and Style Checklist
text: **A. Rewrite using the word in brackets.**
**B. Improve two sentences from your task using a new technique.**
**Style checklist**
bullets: As soon as I closed my eyes, the alarm went off. (No sooner) → ___________________________
She had only just left when the parcel arrived. (Hardly) → ___________________________
I was going to call him, but the line went dead. (about) → ___________________________
After he had checked the windows, he went upstairs. (Having) → ___________________________
I had never felt so alone before. (Never) → ___________________________
I didn't understand what had happened until I saw the letter. (Only when) → ___________________________
He heard the scream and ran outside. (Hearing) → ___________________________
We had just started eating when the power went off. (Scarcely) → ___________________________
I didn't realise he was lying until much later. (Not until) → ___________________________
The moment she opened the box, she screamed. (No sooner) → ___________________________

rows: A very short sentence after a long one

blocks.heading: Answer Key
text: **Handout 3 (examples)**
**Handout 4, Exercise A**
**Common errors to watch for**
bullets: Participle clause: *Having fumbled for my keys in the dark* (adds detail and tension, speeds up the action)
One-word sentence: *Nothing.* / *Empty.* (creates a shock and a pause)
*was about to ... when*: *I was about to call out when I heard it* (interrupts the action)
Negative inversion: *Never had the staircase seemed so long* (emphasises fear)
Delaying: *I was halfway up ... when I noticed* (builds tension)
*No sooner ... than*: *No sooner had I let out a breath than the phone began to ring* (a sudden twist)
Auxiliary + subject (*had I*) · 2. than · 3. when · 4. Dangling participle: the lights didn't lock the door. Correct: *Having locked the door, she turned off the lights.*
No sooner had I closed my eyes than the alarm went off.
Hardly had she left when the parcel arrived.
I was about to call him when the line went dead.
Having checked the windows, he went upstairs.
Never (before) had I felt so alone.
Only when I saw the letter did I understand what had happened.
Hearing the scream, he ran outside.
Scarcely had we started eating when the power went off.
Not until much later did I realise he was lying.
No sooner had she opened the box than she screamed.

rows: No sooner I had arrived than ...
No sooner had I arrived than ...
Hardly had she left than he came.
Hardly had she left when he came.
Having locked the door, the lights went out.
Having locked the door, she turned off the lights.

blocks.title: First and Second Conditionals · Level B1 · About 35 minutes

blocks.heading: Task 1. First conditional
text: Complete with the present simple or will / won't.
Example: If it **rains** (rain), we **will stay** (stay) at home.
numbered: If you ________ (not hurry), you ________ (miss) the bus.
If she ________ (pass) the test, her parents ________ (be) very happy.
We ________ (not go) to the beach if the weather ________ (be) bad.

blocks.heading: Task 2. Second conditional
text: Complete with the past simple or would / wouldn't.
Example: If I **had** (have) more time, I **would learn** (learn) the guitar.
numbered: If I ________ (be) you, I ________ (talk) to the teacher.
She ________ (travel) more if she ________ (not have) a small child.
If we ________ (live) near the sea, we ________ (swim) every day.
They ________ (not complain) if the food ________ (be) better.

blocks.heading: Task 3. Which one?
text: Choose the first or the second conditional, and write the sentence. Ask yourself: is this a real possibility?
Example: (my bus is late most days) If the bus ________ late again, I ________ walk. → If the bus is late again, I will walk.
numbered: (I have no money for a trip) If I ________ (have) the money, I ________ (go) to Japan.
(there is a test next week) If I ________ (study) every evening, I ________ (pass) it.
(I am not the head teacher) If I ________ (be) the head teacher, I ________ (change) the timetable.
(rain is forecast for tomorrow) If it ________ (rain), the match ________ (be) cancelled.

blocks.heading: Task 4. Commas
text: Write each sentence the other way round, and punctuate it correctly.
Example: If I see her, I'll tell her. → I'll tell her if I see her.
numbered: If you need help, ask me. → ________________________
I would buy a bicycle if I lived closer. → ________________________
If we left now, we would arrive before dark. → ________________________
She'll be angry if you forget again. → ________________________

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn: give advice
text: Write advice for each problem using If I were you, I'd ... Then write one first conditional sentence about your own week.
bullets: A friend is always late for class. → ________________________
Your cousin wants to learn English quickly. → ________________________
Someone has lost their phone at school. → ________________________

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: 1 don't hurry / will miss  2 will call / finish  3 passes / will be  4 won't go / is  5 will ... do / say
1 were / would talk  2 would travel / didn't have  3 lived / would swim  4 would ... say / asked  5 wouldn't complain / were

1 If I had the money, I would go to Japan. (unreal)  2 If I study every evening, I will pass it. (real)  3 If I were the head teacher, I would change the timetable. (unreal)  4 If it rains, the match will be cancelled. (real)

1 Ask me if you need help.  2 If I lived closer, I would buy a bicycle.  3 We would arrive before dark if we left now.  4 If you forget again, she'll be angry. (Comma only when the if-clause comes first.)
Answers will vary. Check: *If I were you, I'd* + base verb; and the first conditional sentence has a present tense after if, never will.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 25 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.
**The one to watch:** *will* after *if*. It is the most persistent mistake in the whole B1 syllabus, and it appears in Tasks 1, 3 and 5. One rule on the board beats twenty corrections.
**If I were or if I was:** *were* is the form expected in exams and in writing, and *was* is very common in speech. Teach *were*, and do not mark *was* wrong when a learner says it aloud.
**Task 3 is the thinking task.** Learners who can do Tasks 1 and 2 but not Task 3 have the forms without the meaning, which is exactly what to spend the next lesson on.
**Extension:** learners write three dilemmas of their own and swap them with a partner, who answers each with one conditional sentence.

blocks.title: Passive Voice · Level B1 · About 35 minutes

blocks.heading: Task 1. The third form
text: Write the past participle of each verb.
Example: build → built

blocks.heading: Task 2. Complete the passive
text: Use the present or past simple passive of the verb in brackets.
Example: The bridge **was built** (build) in 1908.
numbered: Rice ________ (grow) in many parts of Asia.

blocks.heading: Task 3. Active to passive
text: Rewrite each sentence in the passive. Leave out the doer if it adds nothing.
Example: Somebody cleans the office every evening. → The office is cleaned every evening.
numbered: Farmers grow tea on these hills. → ________________________
Someone stole my phone at the station. → ________________________
The council checks the water twice a year. → ________________________
Millions of people watch this programme. → ________________________

blocks.heading: Task 4. With by, or without?
text: Decide whether the doer is worth keeping. Write the sentence with by ... or without it.
Example: The window was broken (by somebody). → The window was broken.
numbered: This novel was written (by a teenager). → ________________________
The room is cleaned (by a cleaner). → ________________________
The bridge is used (by thousands of drivers). → ________________________

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Describe a process you know in six sentences: how something is made, grown, cooked or organised. Use the passive where the doer is not important.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: made, written, taken, grown, sent, repaired, spoken, found.
1 is grown  2 were sent  3 is cleaned  4 was stolen  5 are made  6 have not been published (or: were not published)  7 Were ... repaired

1 The school was built in 1975.  2 Tea is grown on these hills.  3 My phone was stolen at the station.  4 The water is checked twice a year.  5 This programme is watched by millions of people. (Here the doer is worth keeping.)

1 This novel was written by a teenager. (Keep: it is the surprise.)  2 The room is cleaned. (Drop: obvious.)  3 The bridge is used by thousands of drivers. (Keep: it is information.)  4 My car was repaired. (Drop: says nothing.)
Answers will vary. Check: be is present in every passive sentence, the participle is the third form, and by is used only where the doer matters.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 25 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.

**The one to watch:** the missing *be* (*the school built in 1975*) and the past simple used instead of the participle (*was build*). Both come from the same place - the passive needs two parts, and learners produce one.

**Task 2, item 6** accepts two answers. *Have not been published* is the present perfect passive and is what a fluent speaker would say with *yet*; *were not published* is acceptable at B1. Praise the first if it appears.
**Task 4 is the thinking task.** Learners who keep every *by* have the form but not the purpose, and that is what makes passive writing sound wrong.
**Extension:** learners rewrite a short paragraph from their coursebook in the passive and decide whether it is improved. Often it is not, and noticing that is the point.

blocks.title: Past Simple · Level A2 · About 35 minutes

blocks.heading: Task 1. Regular or irregular?
text: These verbs are from the story about Lina. Write R (regular) or I (irregular) next to each one. The first one is done for you.
Example: visited → R
bullets: got ____
caught ____
took ____
listened ____
read ____
arrived ____
cooked ____
walked ____
left ____
found ____
enjoyed ____

blocks.heading: Task 2. Write the past simple form
text: Write the past simple of each verb. Be careful with spelling.
Example: play → played

blocks.heading: Task 3. Complete the sentences
text: Use the past simple of the verb in brackets. Some sentences are negative or questions.
Example: I **watched** (watch) a film last night.
numbered: We ________ (not go) to school on Monday.
They ________ (not like) the food at the new café.
Kenji ________ (study) for his test all evening.

blocks.heading: Task 4. Three sounds
text: Say the verbs aloud. Write each one under the sound of its -ed ending.
bullets: Verbs to sort: watched, called, needed, cooked, listened, visited

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Write five sentences about what you did yesterday. Use at least one negative. Then write two questions to ask a partner about their day.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: Regular: listened, arrived, cooked, walked, enjoyed. Irregular: got, caught, took, read, left, found.
watched, studied, stopped, arrived, went, had, saw, bought, made, wrote.
1 didn't go  2 Did ... see  3 bought  4 didn't like  5 did ... go  6 studied  7 stopped  8 didn't have
/t/: worked, watched, cooked. /d/: played, called, listened. /ɪd/: wanted, needed, visited.
Answers will vary. Check: past forms correct, didn't + base verb in negatives, did + subject + base verb in questions.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 25 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.
**Common mistakes:** *didn't went*, *did you saw*, *goed*, and saying walked as two syllables. Task 3 items 1, 4 and 8 and Task 4 target exactly these.
**Using it:** learners check Tasks 1 to 3 in pairs before you give the answers, so every learner explains at least one answer aloud.
**Extension:** learners swap their Task 5 questions with a partner and answer them in full sentences, then report one answer to the class.

hero.text: A printable present perfect worksheet for B1 learners: past participles, have and has, the contrast with the past simple, questions with ever, and a writing task about their own experiences. Full answer key and teacher's notes.

blocks.heading: About this worksheet
text: It goes with the Present Perfect lesson plan but works on its own, in class or as homework.

blocks.label: Print this worksheet
blocks.note: Prints without the site's menus or advertisements.

blocks.title: Present Perfect · Level B1 · About 35 minutes

blocks.heading: Task 1. The third form
text: Write the past simple and the past participle of each verb.
Example: go → went → gone

blocks.heading: Task 2. have or has
text: Complete the sentences with have, has, haven't or hasn't, and the verb in brackets.
Example: She **has done** (do) a first-aid course.
numbered: We ________ ________ (know) each other since primary school.

blocks.heading: Task 3. Present perfect or past simple?
text: Choose the right tense. Look for a time expression: if the sentence says when, use the past simple.
Example: I **have been** to three countries. (No time is given, so it is the present perfect.)
numbered: My aunt ________ (teach) me to swim when I was six.
He ________ (work) here for two years, and he is still here.

blocks.heading: Task 4. Ask and answer
text: Write a question with Have you ever ...? and a true short answer for yourself.
Example: sleep / in a tent → Have you ever slept in a tent? - Yes, I have.

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Write five true sentences about your own experiences. Use never in two of them. Then add one sentence in the past simple giving the time of one experience.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: do/did/done; see/saw/seen; eat/ate/eaten; write/wrote/written; break/broke/broken; take/took/taken; study/studied/studied; swim/swam/swum; lose/lost/lost.
1 have never visited  2 Have ... ever ridden  3 hasn't finished  4 have known  5 Have ... ever worked  6 has lost
1 has lived  2 moved  3 Have ... met  4 haven't seen  5 taught  6 has worked
Have you ever cooked for ten people? / broken a bone? / forgotten someone's name? / swum in the sea? / won a competition? Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, I haven't. (not "Yes, I have ever")
Answers will vary. Check: have/has + past participle, never before the participle, and the past simple sentence has a time expression.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 25 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.
**The one to watch:** a finished time with the present perfect (*I have been there last year*). Task 3 is built on exactly this, so mark it carefully and ask learners *why*, not just *what*.
**been or gone:** if learners ask, *has been to* means they went and came back; *has gone to* means they are still there. Task 1 gives the forms; the difference is worth two minutes on the board.
**American usage:** *Did you ever see it?* is normal in American English. It is not wrong, but international exams expect *Have you ever seen it?*, and that is what Task 4 practises.
**Extension:** learners turn their Task 4 questions into a class survey and report the results: *Four of us have swum in the sea.*

blocks.title: Present Simple · Level A1 · About 35 minutes

blocks.heading: Task 1. Add the -s
text: Write the he/she/it form of each verb. Be careful with spelling.
Example: work → works

blocks.heading: Task 2. Positive, negative, question
text: Complete the sentences with the present simple of the verb in brackets.
Example: She **works** (work) in a bakery.

blocks.heading: Task 3. How often?
text: Put the frequency word in the right place and write the whole sentence.
Example: (always) She gets up at five. → She always gets up at five.
numbered: (always) I am tired in the evening. → ________________________

blocks.heading: Task 4. Three sounds
text: Say the verbs aloud. Write each one under the sound of its ending.
bullets: Verbs to sort: reads, watches, starts, goes, teaches, eats

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Write eight sentences about one person in your family: their routine, what they do not do, and how often. Use at least two negatives.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: eats, goes, watches, studies, plays, finishes, has, teaches, lives.
1 studies  2 don't live  3 Does ... drive  4 doesn't eat  5 Do ... speak  6 opens  7 don't like
1 He never eats meat.  2 We usually walk to school.  3 My sister is often late.  4 They sometimes play football on Friday.  5 I am always tired in the evening. (After be, the adverb goes second.)
/s/: works, starts, eats. /z/: lives, reads, goes. /ɪz/: finishes, watches, teaches.
Answers will vary. Check: -s on every third-person verb, don't/doesn't + verb with no ending, frequency words before the main verb.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 25 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.
**The one to watch:** the missing -s in Task 2 and Task 5, and the *extra* -s after doesn't (*she doesn't works*). Both are worth one minute on the board rather than a correction on each script.

**Task 3, item 5** is the exception: after *be*, the frequency word comes after the verb. Learners who put *always* first have applied the rule they were taught, so praise the logic before correcting.
**Using it:** learners check Tasks 1 to 3 in pairs before you give answers, and read the sentence aloud when they check, so the ending is heard as well as written.
**Extension:** learners swap their Task 5 paragraph and write three questions about the person described.

hero.text: A printable reported speech worksheet for B1 learners: said and told, statements, reported questions, and the changes to tense, pronouns and time words, ending with a task using things people really said to them. Full answer key and teacher's notes.

blocks.heading: About this worksheet
text: It goes with the Reported Speech lesson plan but works on its own, in class or as homework.

blocks.label: Print this worksheet
blocks.note: Prints without the site's menus or advertisements.

blocks.title: Reported Speech · Level B1 · About 40 minutes

blocks.heading: Task 1. said or told?
text: Complete each sentence with said or told.
Example: She **told** me that she was tired.
numbered: He ________ that the shop was closed.
They ________ us the bus had already left.
My teacher ________ that we could leave early.
The doctor ________ her to rest for a week.

blocks.heading: Task 2. Report the statement
text: Rewrite each sentence as reported speech. Change the tense, the pronouns and the time words.
Example: "I am busy today," she said. → She said that she was busy that day.
numbered: "I will call you tomorrow," he said. → ________________________
"I finished the book yesterday," he told me. → ________________________
"We are waiting outside," they told us. → ________________________

blocks.heading: Task 3. Report the question
text: Rewrite each question as a reported question. Remember: no do, does or did, and no question word order.
Example: "Where do you live?" she asked. → She asked where I lived.
numbered: "What time does the film start?" he asked. → ________________________
"Have you seen my keys?" she asked. → ________________________
"Why did you leave early?" they asked. → ________________________
"Are you coming with us?" he asked. → ________________________

blocks.heading: Task 4. Find the mistake
text: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
Example: He said me that he was late. → He told me that he was late.
numbered: She asked where did I work. → ________________________
They told that the office was closed. → ________________________
He said he will help me tomorrow. → ________________________
She asked me do I like the food. → ________________________

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Write five sentences reporting things people really said to you today or yesterday. Use said at least twice, told at least twice, and asked at least once.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: 1 They said that they lived in Colombo.  2 He said that he would call me the next day.  3 She said that she couldn't swim.  4 He told me that he had finished the book the day before.  5 They told us that they were waiting outside.

1 He asked what time the film started.  2 She asked whether/if I had seen her keys.  3 They asked why I had left early.  4 He asked whether/if I was going with them.  5 The teacher asked who had written it. (With who as the subject, the word order does not change.)
1 She asked where I worked.  2 They said that the office was closed. (or: They told me that ...)  3 He said he would help me the next day.  4 She asked me whether/if I liked the food.
Answers will vary. Check: told always has a person after it, said does not; reported questions have statement word order and no did.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 30 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.

**The one to watch:** question word order in Task 3 (*she asked where did I live*). If most of the class does this, stop and put one pair of sentences on the board rather than correcting thirty scripts.
**Task 3, item 5** is worth showing to everyone: when the question word is the subject (*who wrote this?*), the word order was never inverted, so nothing moves.

**A fair point learners raise:** *She said she lives in Kandy* is also correct if she still lives there. The backshifted form is never wrong, so teach it first and accept the other when a learner can explain why.
**Extension:** learners write a short dialogue of six lines, swap with a partner, and report their partner's dialogue in a paragraph.

hero.text: A printable A1 grammar worksheet on the present continuous: building the form, the spelling of *-ing*, negatives and questions, and choosing between the present simple and the present continuous. Five tasks, a full answer key and teacher's notes.

blocks.heading: About this worksheet
text: This is the tense for what is happening now, in front of the learner, which makes it the easiest tense to teach and the easiest to practise: everything in the room is available as an example.

blocks.label: Print this worksheet
blocks.note: Prints without the site's menus or advertisements.

blocks.title: Grammar: Present Continuous · Level A1 · About 35 minutes
How to build it
text: **The form is two parts:** *am*, *is* or *are*, then the verb with **-ing**. *I am working. He is reading. They are waiting.* Both parts are needed - **He reading** and **He is read** are both wrong.
**Short forms are normal in speech:** *I'm working, he's reading, they're waiting, we aren't listening, she isn't coming.*
**Negatives** put *not* in the middle: *I am not working. She is not (isn't) coming. We are not (aren't) listening.*
**Questions** turn the first two words round: *Are you working? Is he reading? What are they doing?* Answer short: *Yes, I am. No, he isn't.*

**Spelling of -ing:** most verbs just add it - *work - working*. Verbs ending in one **-e** drop it: *write - writing, make - making*. One short vowel and one consonant at the end doubles the consonant: *sit - sitting, run - running, swim - swimming*.
**Now, not always.** Use the present continuous for what is happening at this moment, and the present simple for what happens every day: *I am eating rice* (now) but *I eat rice every day* (always).

blocks.heading: Task 1. Write the -ing form
text: Write the -ing form of each verb. Be careful with the spelling.
Example: work → **working**

blocks.heading: Task 2. Am, is or are?
text: Complete each sentence with am, is or are and the verb in brackets.
Example: She **is reading** a book. (read)
bullets: I ________ to the radio. (listen)
They ________ football in the garden. (play)
My mother ________ dinner. (cook)
We ________ for the bus. (wait)
The baby ________ . (sleep)
You ________ very fast! (write)

blocks.heading: Task 3. Negatives and questions
text: Make each sentence negative, then make a question from it.
Example: He is watching television. → Negative: **He isn't watching television.** Question: **Is he watching television?**

blocks.heading: Task 4. Now or every day?
text: Choose the right form: present simple or present continuous.
Example: Look! It **is raining**. (rain)
bullets: I ________ to school every morning. (walk)
Be quiet - the baby ________ . (sleep)
My father ________ in a bank. (work)
What ________ you ________ at the moment? (do)
We usually ________ dinner at seven. (have)
She can't come to the phone. She ________ a shower. (have)

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Look around you. Write six sentences about what people near you are doing right now. Use a different verb each time.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: reading; writing; sitting. running; making; playing. swimming; coming; studying.
1 am listening  2 are playing  3 is cooking  4 are waiting  5 is sleeping  6 are writing

1 They aren't studying English. / Are they studying English?  2 She isn't wearing a red dress. / Is she wearing a red dress?  3 I'm not sitting in the right seat. / Am I sitting in the right seat?  4 The children aren't playing outside. / Are the children playing outside?
1 walk  2 is sleeping  3 works  4 are ... doing  5 have  6 is having
Answers will vary. Check both parts of the form - *is* or *are* plus *-ing* - and the spelling of any doubled consonant.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 25 minutes; Task 5 about 10.
**Teach it standing up.** Mime an action and ask *What am I doing?* Four or five actions and the whole class has the form before any writing. This tense does not need a text.

**The missing verb to be is the error to watch.** *He reading* is what learners produce for months, because many languages need no equivalent. Insist on both parts from the first lesson, and point at the two parts on the board every time.
**Spelling is half the marks lost.** *Siting*, *runing*, *writeing*: do Task 1 before anything else and check it as a class.
**Task 4 is the hard one, and it is worth the time.** The question to ask each item is *now, or always?* Learners who ask that question get it right; learners who look for a keyword do not.
**Extension:** one learner mimes, the class writes the sentence. Ten actions, ten sentences, and every one is a real answer about something they can see.

blocks.heading: About this worksheet
text: Comparing is one of the first genuinely useful things a learner can do with English: cheaper, faster, the best one in the shop. The forms are simple; the errors are predictable, and this sheet targets them.

blocks.label: Print this worksheet
blocks.note: Prints without the site's menus or advertisements.

blocks.title: Grammar: Comparatives and Superlatives · Level A2 · About 40 minutes
How the two forms are built
text: **Short adjectives (one syllable)** add **-er** and **-est**: *cheap - cheaper - the cheapest*. If the word ends in one vowel and one consonant, double the consonant: *big - bigger - the biggest*. If it ends in **-y**, change it to **i**: *easy - easier - the easiest*. Two-syllable words ending in -y follow this too: *happy - happier - the happiest*.
**Long adjectives (two syllables or more)** use **more** and **the most**: *expensive - more expensive - the most expensive*. Never both at once: **more cheaper** is wrong.
**Four common words are irregular:** *good - better - the best*, *bad - worse - the worst*, *far - further - the furthest*, *little - less - the least*.

**The two small words that carry the meaning.** Use **than** after a comparative - *This bag is cheaper than that one* - and **the** before a superlative - *It is the cheapest in the shop*. For things that are equal, use **as ... as**: *My bag is as heavy as yours*.

blocks.heading: Task 1. Build the forms
text: Write the comparative and the superlative of each adjective.
Example: cheap → **cheaper** · **the cheapest**

blocks.heading: Task 2. Comparative or superlative?
text: Put the adjective in brackets into the right form. Add than or the where you need them.
Example: A bicycle is **cheaper than** a motorbike. (cheap)
bullets: My brother is ________ me, but my sister is ________ in the family. (tall / tall)
This is ________ book I have ever read. (interesting)
The bus is ________ the train, but it takes longer. (cheap)
Yesterday was ________ day of the year. (hot)
Her handwriting is ________ mine. (bad)
Which is ________ way to the station, the road or the path? (short)

blocks.heading: Task 3. Say it another way
text: Rewrite each sentence using the word in brackets, so it means the same.
Example: My bag is heavier than yours. (lighter) → **Your bag is lighter than mine.**
bullets: The red shirt is cheaper than the blue one. (expensive) → ____________________
No mountain in the country is higher than this one. (highest) → ____________________
My father is 45. My mother is 45. (as ... as) → ____________________
The film was not as good as the book. (better) → ____________________

blocks.heading: Task 4. Find and correct the mistake
text: Each sentence has one mistake. Cross it out and write the correct form.
Example: This is ~~the most cheapest~~ **the cheapest** one in the shop.
bullets: My new phone is more better than the old one. ____________
She is the most tall girl in the class. ____________
This exercise is more easy than the last one. ____________
Colombo is bigger that Kandy. ____________
He is the worse driver I know. ____________
My house is as big than yours. ____________

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Write six sentences comparing things you know: two places, two kinds of food, two ways of travelling, two subjects at school. Use three comparatives and three superlatives, and underline them.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: 1 hotter / the hottest.  2 heavier / the heaviest.  3 more careful / the most careful.  4 better / the best.  5 further (or farther) / the furthest.  6 more interesting / the most interesting.
1 taller than ... the tallest  2 the most interesting  3 cheaper than  4 the hottest  5 worse than  6 the shortest
Suggested answers. 1 The blue shirt is more expensive than the red one. 2 This is the highest mountain in the country. 3 My father is as old as my mother. 4 The book was better than the film.
1 better than (not *more better*)  2 the tallest  3 easier  4 bigger than  5 the worst  6 as big as
Answers will vary. Check for *than* after every comparative, *the* before every superlative, and no *more* beside an -er form.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 30 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.

**Count the syllables out loud.** Learners who clap the syllables choose between *-er* and *more* correctly far more often than learners given the rule in writing. Two syllables is the hard case: *careful* takes *more*, but *happy* takes *-er*.
**The double mistake is the one to name:** *more better*, *more easier*, *the most cheapest*. One form or the other, never both. Write two on the board wrong and let the class repair them.
**Than and that** sound almost the same in fast speech, which is why *bigger that Kandy* appears in writing. Drill the sentence aloud, then write it.
**Do Task 3 in pairs.** Saying the same idea from the other side - *heavier* to *lighter* - is what shows whether learners have the meaning or only the ending.
**Extension:** learners write three true and three false comparisons about the class or the town, swap, and correct their partner's false ones with a full sentence.

hero.text: A printable A2 grammar worksheet on *in*, *on* and *at* for time and place: sorting, gap-fill, error correction, a short description and a writing task. Full answer key and teacher's notes.

blocks.heading: About this worksheet
text: Prepositions are learnt one phrase at a time rather than by rule, so this worksheet gives the three patterns that do cover most cases and then practises the phrases that have to be remembered.

blocks.label: Print this worksheet
blocks.note: Prints without the site's menus or advertisements.

blocks.title: Grammar: Prepositions of Time and Place · Level A2 · About 40 minutes
The pattern behind in, on and at
text: For **time**, the three words work from large to small. **In** takes the big containers: *in 2026, in March, in the morning, in winter*. **On** takes days and dates: *on Monday, on 3 May, on my birthday, on Friday evening*. **At** takes clock times and two or three fixed phrases: *at six o'clock, at night, at the weekend, at Christmas*.

For **place**, the same shape holds: **in** for something with sides around it - *in a room, in a car, in Colombo, in the water*; **on** for a surface or a line - *on the table, on the wall, on the bus, on the third floor*; **at** for a point you think of as a place you are - *at school, at the bus stop, at the door, at work*.
Two phrases break the pattern and simply have to be learnt: *in the morning* but *at night*, and *in a car* but *on a bus*.

blocks.heading: Task 1. Sort the phrases
text: Write each phrase in the right column: IN, ON or AT.
Example: Monday → **ON**
bullets: half past seven ____    ·    July ____    ·    the weekend ____
my birthday ____    ·    2019 ____    ·    night ____
the afternoon ____    ·    14 April ____    ·    Christmas Day ____
the table ____    ·    the bus stop ____    ·    the kitchen ____
the second floor ____    ·    school ____    ·    Kandy ____

blocks.heading: Task 2. Time: fill the gap
text: Write in, on or at.
Example: The class starts **at** nine o'clock.
bullets: My sister was born ____ 2011.
We always visit my grandmother ____ Sunday.
I do my homework ____ the evening, but ____ night I read.
The shop is closed ____ the weekend.
The examination is ____ 12 December, ____ half past eight.
It rains a lot here ____ November.

blocks.heading: Task 3. Place: fill the gap
text: Write in, on or at.
Example: Your bag is **on** the chair.
bullets: There were twenty people ____ the bus.
She is waiting ____ the door.
We keep the rice ____ that cupboard.
My uncle works ____ a bank ____ Galle.
The picture is ____ the wall, above the clock.
I met him ____ the bus stop, not ____ the station.

blocks.heading: Task 4. Find and correct the mistake
text: Each sentence has one wrong preposition. Cross it out and write the right one.
Example: I get up at six o'clock ~~in~~ **on** weekdays.
bullets: We arrived in Monday morning. ____
My birthday is in the fifth of June. ____
She lives on Colombo with her aunt. ____
I read for an hour in night. ____
There is nobody on the classroom. ____
The bus leaves in ten o'clock. ____

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Write six sentences about your own week. Use in, on and at at least twice each, and underline them.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: AT: half past seven, the weekend, night, the bus stop, school, Christmas Day (also *on* Christmas Day - accept both). IN: July, 2019, the afternoon, the kitchen, Kandy. ON: my birthday, 14 April, the table, the second floor.
1 in  2 on  3 in ... at  4 at  5 on ... at  6 in
1 on  2 at  3 in  4 in ... in  5 on  6 at ... at
1 on Monday morning  2 on the fifth of June  3 in Colombo  4 at night  5 in the classroom  6 at ten o'clock
Answers will vary. Check that each preposition matches the pattern in the box, and that *at night* and *on Monday* are right, as those are the two most often wrong.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 30 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.

**Teach it as phrases, not as rules.** *At night* and *on the bus* break the pattern, and no explanation will fix them - only meeting them often. Get learners to record the whole phrase in their notebooks, never the preposition alone.

**Do Task 1 in pairs, out loud.** Learners argue about *Christmas Day* and *the weekend*, and the argument teaches more than the answer. Both *at Christmas* and *on Christmas Day* are correct, and it is worth saying why: one is the season, the other is the date.
**Task 4 is the diagnostic task.** If learners get Tasks 2 and 3 right but fail Task 4, they can apply a rule but not notice a mistake, which is exactly what an examination asks for. Slow down here.
**Two errors are worth a minute each:** *in Monday* (the commonest time error) and *on the classroom* (the commonest place error). Put both on the board wrong and let the class repair them.
**Extension:** learners write five true sentences and three false ones about their week, swap papers, and find the false ones. They read far more carefully when there is something hidden.

hero.text: A printable B2 grammar worksheet on relative clauses: which pronoun to use, when the commas change the meaning, when the pronoun can be left out, and combining short sentences into one. Five tasks, a full answer key and teacher's notes.

blocks.heading: About this worksheet
text: Relative clauses are what let a writer put two ideas in one sentence instead of two, which is most of the difference between B1 writing and B2 writing. The grammar is not hard; the comma rule carries real meaning and is worth the time.

blocks.label: Print this worksheet
blocks.note: Prints without the site's menus or advertisements.

blocks.title: Grammar: Relative Clauses · Level B2 · About 50 minutes
Defining, non-defining, and the commas that separate them
text: **A defining clause** says which one you mean, and the sentence loses its sense without it. No commas: *The teacher who taught me French has retired.* (Which teacher? That one.) Use *who* for people, *which* for things, *that* for either, *whose* for possession, *where* for places and *when* for times.

**A non-defining clause** adds extra information about something already identified. Commas, always: *Mrs Perera, who taught me French, has retired.* We already know who she is; the clause is an aside. **That** is not used here, and the commas are not optional.

**The commas change the meaning.** *The students who failed must retake the paper* means only some failed. *The students, who failed, must retake the paper* means all of them did. Read both aloud and the pause does the same work as the commas.

**You can leave the pronoun out** when it is the object of a defining clause: *The book (which) I read last week*. You cannot leave it out when it is the subject - *The man who lives next door* keeps its *who* - and never in a non-defining clause.
**Which can also refer to a whole clause**, in writing: *He arrived two hours late, which annoyed everybody.* Here *which* means the whole of what went before, not one noun.

blocks.heading: Task 1. Choose the pronoun
text: Write who, which, that, whose, where or when. Where more than one is possible, write both.
Example: That is the shop **which / that** sells the best bread.
bullets: The woman ________ car was stolen has gone to the police.
This is the village ________ my mother grew up.
Is that the man ________ you were telling me about?
2019 was the year ________ the factory closed.
My neighbour, ________ works nights, sleeps until two.
He failed the examination, ________ surprised nobody.

blocks.heading: Task 2. Commas or no commas?
text: Add commas where they are needed. Two sentences need none. Then say what each sentence means.
Example: My sister who lives in Galle is a nurse. → **My sister, who lives in Galle, is a nurse.** (I have one sister.) Without commas it would mean I have more than one.
bullets: The bus which leaves at six is always full. ____________
Our head teacher who has been here for twenty years is retiring. ____________
The parcel that arrived this morning was not for us. ____________
Kandy which is in the hills is much cooler than Colombo. ____________
The people who complained have been given their money back. ____________

blocks.heading: Task 3. Make one sentence
text: Join each pair using a relative clause. Use commas where the extra information is not needed to identify anything.
Example: I met a woman. She had lived in five countries. → **I met a woman who had lived in five countries.**
bullets: The film was three hours long. We saw it on Friday. → ____________________
My uncle has sold his shop. He is seventy next month. → ____________________
I still use the dictionary. My father gave it to me. → ____________________
The hotel was fully booked. We wanted to stay there. → ____________________
She missed the train. This meant she missed the interview. → ____________________

blocks.heading: Task 4. Find and correct the mistake
text: Each sentence has one mistake. Cross it out and write the correction.
Example: My brother, ~~that~~ **who** lives in Jaffna, is a doctor.
bullets: The man which repaired my laptop was very quick. ____________
The house where I was born in has been pulled down. ____________
Students who they arrive late will not be admitted. ____________
Ella, that is famous for its views, is two hours away. ____________
This is the book I told you about it. ____________
My best friend who I have known since we were six is getting married. ____________

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Write six sentences about people and places you know, using six different relative pronouns. At least two must be non-defining, with commas, and at least one must use which to refer to a whole clause.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: 1 whose  2 where  3 who / that (or no pronoun: *the man you were telling me about*)  4 when  5 who (non-defining, so not *that*)  6 which

1 No commas: it says which bus. 2 Commas: *Our head teacher, who has been here for twenty years, is retiring* - a school has one head teacher. 3 No commas: it says which parcel. 4 Commas: *Kandy, which is in the hills, ...* - there is only one Kandy. 5 No commas: only the people who complained, not everyone.

Suggested answers. 1 The film (which/that) we saw on Friday was three hours long. 2 My uncle, who is seventy next month, has sold his shop. 3 I still use the dictionary (which/that) my father gave me. 4 The hotel (which/that) we wanted to stay at was fully booked. 5 She missed the train, which meant she missed the interview.

1 who/that repaired my laptop  2 the house where I was born (or *which I was born in*) - not both  3 Students who arrive late (no *they*)  4 Ella, which is famous ... (*that* is not used in non-defining clauses)  5 the book I told you about (no *it*)  6 My best friend, who I have known since we were six, is getting married (commas: you have one best friend)
Answers will vary. Check three things: no *that* in a non-defining clause, commas at both ends or neither, and no repeated object - *the book which I read it* is the commonest error at this level.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 35 minutes; Task 5 about 15, or set it as homework.

**Teach the commas as meaning, not as punctuation.** Put *My sister who lives in Galle* and *My sister, who lives in Galle* on the board and ask how many sisters the writer has. Learners who see that the commas change the facts stop treating them as decoration.
**Read the pairs aloud.** A non-defining clause has a pause and a drop in pitch at each comma; a defining clause runs straight through. Hearing it is faster than any rule.
**The repeated object is the error to hunt.** *The book which I read it*, *the man who I spoke to him*: most learners' first languages allow this, so it survives long after the pronouns are secure.

**Task 3 is where B2 writing is built.** Ask for the joined sentence aloud first, then written. Learners who can join two sentences aloud write noticeably longer, better-linked paragraphs within a few weeks.

**Extension:** learners take a paragraph from their own recent writing and combine every pair of short sentences that share a noun. They usually find three or four, and the paragraph improves visibly.
