blocks.heading: About this worksheet
text: It practises the four things reading questions really test - finding facts, working out a word from its context, understanding why somebody did something, and reading the question properly.

blocks.label: Print this worksheet
blocks.note: Prints without the site's menus or advertisements.

blocks.title: Reading Comprehension: The Night Market · Level A2 · About 40 minutes
The night market
text: **1** Every Friday evening, the square behind the bus station changes. At five o'clock it is an empty car park. By seven it is the busiest place in town. Families come to eat, students come to meet their friends, and the whole square smells of frying onions and sweet tea.

**2** Ravi has sold fruit there for eleven years. He arrives at four with his brother and they build the stall together: four poles, a plastic roof and two tables. "The building takes an hour," he says, "and the selling takes five." His busiest hour is between eight and nine, when people finish work.
**3** Not everyone comes to buy. Mariam, who is sixteen, comes with three friends every week. "We can't afford much," she says. "We buy one plate of noodles and share it. We come for the noise."

**4** By midnight the stalls are gone. Ravi and his brother take down the poles, sweep the ground and drive home. On Saturday morning the square is a car park again, and nobody would know that four thousand people stood there the night before.

blocks.heading: Task 1. True or false?
text: Write T or F. Find the words in the text that gave you the answer.
Example: The market happens every Friday evening. → T
bullets: The square is a car park during the day. ____
Ravi works at the market alone. ____
It takes Ravi one hour to build his stall. ____
Mariam and her friends buy a plate of noodles each. ____
The stalls stay in the square all night. ____

blocks.heading: Task 2. Choose the best answer
text: Circle a, b or c.
Example: The market is behind: a) the school  b) **the bus station**  c) the hospital
bullets: Ravi has worked at the market for: a) four years  b) five years  c) eleven years
His busiest time is: a) five to six  b) eight to nine  c) after midnight
Mariam comes to the market mainly to: a) buy food  b) meet her friends and enjoy the noise  c) help her family
On Saturday morning the square is: a) full of stalls  b) closed  c) a car park again

blocks.heading: Task 3. Answer in your own words
text: Write one full sentence for each. Do not copy whole sentences from the text.
Example: What time does the market become busy? → It is very busy by seven o'clock in the evening.
bullets: Why does Ravi arrive at four o'clock? ________________________
What does the square smell of? ________________________
Why does Mariam share one plate of noodles? ________________________
What do Ravi and his brother do at the end of the night? ________________________

blocks.heading: Task 4. Words from the text
text: Find a word in the text that means the same as each phrase below. The paragraph is given in brackets.
Example: a small shop with a table, in a market (paragraph 2) → stall
bullets: a place where people leave cars (paragraph 1) → ________
long pieces of wood or metal that hold something up (paragraph 2) → ________
have enough money for something (paragraph 3) → ________
clean the ground with a brush (paragraph 4) → ________

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Write six sentences about a market, a shop or a street you know. Say when it is busy, who goes there, and what you can buy.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: 1 T ("At five o'clock it is an empty car park")  2 F (he arrives with his brother)  3 T ("The building takes an hour")  4 F (they buy one plate and share it)  5 F ("By midnight the stalls are gone")

Suggested answers. 1 Because it takes an hour to build the stall before the market opens. 2 It smells of fried onions and sweet tea. 3 Because she and her friends do not have much money. 4 They take down the poles, sweep the ground and drive home.
Answers will vary. Check: present simple for what usually happens, and at least one sentence saying when it is busy.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 30 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.

**Read the text twice, differently.** First for one minute with one question on the board - *what kind of place is this?* - then again for the tasks. Learners who start on the questions immediately read every word and finish nothing.
**Task 1 asks for the evidence** as well as the answer. That habit - point to the words - is what stops learners answering from what they expect rather than what the text says.
**Task 3 is the hard one:** answering in their own words. Accept any correct answer that is not copied word for word, and praise short answers over long copied ones.
**Task 4 teaches the skill that matters most** in examinations: working out a word from the words around it rather than reaching for a dictionary.
**Extension:** learners write three more comprehension questions on the text and swap them with a partner.

blocks.heading: About this worksheet
text: The step from A2 to B1 reading is the step from *what does it say* to *what does it mean*. Three of the five tasks here ask for something the text does not state in so many words, which is exactly where intermediate learners lose marks.

blocks.label: Print this worksheet
blocks.note: Prints without the site's menus or advertisements.

blocks.title: Reading Comprehension: The Repair Shop · Level B1 · About 45 minutes
The repair shop
text: **1** When Nadika's kettle stopped working, she did what most people do: she looked at the price of a new one. It was 4,200 rupees. Then a neighbour told her about the repair shop at the end of the market, and she carried the kettle there instead, feeling slightly foolish.

**2** The shop is not much more than a table under a roof. Behind it sits Piyal, who has been mending things for thirty-one years - radios at first, then televisions, and now, he says, "mostly kettles, fans and the machines that nobody makes parts for any more." He charged Nadika 600 rupees and told her the kettle would outlive the new one she had been about to buy.
**3** She did not believe him at the time. Two years later the kettle is still boiling water every morning, and she has sent four people to the shop.

**4** Piyal is careful about which jobs he takes. He turns away perhaps one machine in three, usually the newest ones. "They are built so that nobody can open them," he says. "Sometimes there is no screw at all - the case is glued. I can open it, but I cannot close it again, and then the customer blames me." He also refuses anything where the part he needs costs more than half the price of a new machine, which he says is a decision the customer should not have to make twice.

**5** Younger repairers are rare. Piyal trained two, and both now work in phone shops, where the money is better and the work is faster. He does not blame them. But he points out that the market has three shops selling new kettles and one table mending them, and that thirty years ago the numbers were the other way round.

blocks.heading: Task 1. The main idea
text: Choose the sentence that best describes what the whole text is about. Then say in one sentence why the other three are wrong.
bullets: a) A woman's kettle broke and she had it repaired.
b) Repairing things is often cheaper than replacing them, but the trade is disappearing.
c) Modern machines are badly made.
d) Piyal has worked as a repairer for thirty-one years.

blocks.heading: Task 2. Reading for detail
text: Answer in a full sentence. Each answer is stated in the text.
Example: How much did the repair cost? → **It cost 600 rupees.**
bullets: What did Nadika do before she heard about the repair shop? ______________________
What kinds of machine does Piyal mend most often now? ______________________
How many machines does he turn away? ______________________
What happened to the two repairers he trained? ______________________

blocks.heading: Task 3. What the text suggests
text: The text does not say these things directly. Decide whether each one is probably true or probably false, and write the words from the text that made you decide.
Example: Nadika was embarrassed to take an old kettle to be mended. → **Probably true: "feeling slightly foolish".**
bullets: Piyal thinks some machines are designed to be impossible to repair. ______________________
Nadika regrets having the kettle repaired. ______________________
Piyal believes repairing pays as well as working in a phone shop. ______________________
Repair work in the market was more common in the past. ______________________

blocks.heading: Task 4. Vocabulary in context
text: Find the word or phrase in the text that means the same as each of these. The paragraph is in brackets.
Example: repairing (paragraph 2) → **mending**
bullets: live longer than (paragraph 2) → ____________
refuses to accept (paragraph 4) → ____________
stuck together, with no screws (paragraph 4) → ____________
not many, hard to find (paragraph 5) → ____________

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Write 80 to 100 words. Would you repair a machine or replace it? Give two reasons, and mention one thing from the text that you agree or disagree with.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: **b.** (a) and (d) are true but are only details, not what the whole text is about; (c) is an opinion the text does not make - Piyal says new machines are hard to open, which is not the same as badly made.
1 She looked at the price of a new kettle (4,200 rupees). 2 Kettles, fans, and machines nobody makes parts for any more. 3 About one in three. 4 They both went to work in phone shops.

1 Probably true: "They are built so that nobody can open them ... the case is glued." 2 Probably false: the kettle still works and she has sent four people to the shop. 3 Probably false: he says the money is better in phone shops and does not blame them for going. 4 Probably true: "thirty years ago the numbers were the other way round."

Answers will vary. Mark on three things: a clear position, two reasons, and one specific reference to the text. At B1, expect *because*, *however* and *for example* to appear; expect and accept simple sentences.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 30 minutes; Task 5 about 15, or set it as homework.
**Do Task 1 before anything else, with the books closed after one minute of reading.** Main idea is a skimming skill, and learners cannot practise it once they have read every word four times.

**Task 3 is the B1 task.** Inference questions are where intermediate learners lose most marks, and the fix is the second half of the instruction: name the words that made you decide. A guess with no evidence is the habit to break.
**Do not pre-teach the vocabulary in Task 4.** The task is working a meaning out from the words around it. Pre-teaching removes the exercise.

**Expect an argument about question 3 in Task 3.** Learners often say Piyal thinks repairing pays badly *and* that he resents it. The text supports the first and not the second, and that distinction is worth five minutes.
**Extension:** learners write two more inference questions on the text, with the evidence, and swap with a partner.

pages.teaches: Common English collocations: make, do, take, have and get

hero.text: A printable A2 vocabulary worksheet on the words that go together: *make a mistake*, *do the shopping*, *take a photograph*, *have breakfast*, *get better*. Five tasks, a full answer key and teacher's notes.

blocks.heading: About this worksheet
text: Collocation is the difference between correct English and natural English. A learner who says *do a mistake* has broken no grammar rule, and every listener notices. These are learnt as pairs, which is what this sheet practises.

blocks.label: Print this worksheet
blocks.note: Prints without the site's menus or advertisements.

blocks.title: Vocabulary: Everyday Collocations · Level A2 · About 40 minutes
Five verbs that take their own partners
text: **Make** is for things you produce or create: *make a cake, make a noise, make a mistake, make a decision, make friends, make money, make the bed*.
**Do** is for work, jobs and activities in general: *do your homework, do the shopping, do the washing-up, do exercise, do your best, do nothing*.
**Take** is for things you pick up, use or spend: *take a photograph, take a bus, take a shower, take medicine, take an examination, take time*.

**Have** is for meals, experiences and things you possess for a while: *have breakfast, have a shower, have a good time, have a look, have a headache, have a baby*. Note that *have a shower* and *take a shower* are both correct.
**Get** is for changes and for receiving: *get better, get dark, get married, get a letter, get home, get angry, get dressed*.
There is no rule that explains why we say *make a mistake* and *do the shopping*. Learn the two words together - write *make a mistake*, never just *mistake* - and the pairs stay.

blocks.heading: Task 1. Which verb?
text: Write make, do, take, have or get in front of each phrase. Some take more than one - write both.
Example: ____ the shopping → **do** the shopping
bullets: ____ a photograph    ·    ____ a mistake    ·    ____ your homework
____ breakfast    ·    ____ a shower    ·    ____ the bed
____ better    ·    ____ a decision    ·    ____ the bus
____ a headache    ·    ____ the washing-up    ·    ____ married
____ friends    ·    ____ dressed    ·    ____ your best

blocks.heading: Task 2. Complete the sentences
text: Use the right form of make, do, take, have or get. Watch the tense.
Example: I always **have** breakfast at seven.
bullets: Sorry - I ________ a mistake. Let me start again.
It ________ dark very early in December.
She ________ a photograph of the whole class.
Could you ________ the washing-up tonight?
We ________ a really good time at the wedding.
He ________ the bus to work every morning.
Have you ________ your homework yet?

blocks.heading: Task 3. Find and correct the mistake
text: Each sentence has one wrong verb. Cross it out and write the right one.
Example: I ~~did~~ **made** a mistake in the second question.
bullets: She makes her homework every evening. ____________
Can I take a look at your dictionary? ____________
We must do a decision before Friday. ____________
He took a bad cold last week. ____________
I need to do a shower before we go out. ____________
They did friends very quickly. ____________

blocks.heading: Task 4. Match and use
text: Match each beginning on the left with an ending on the right, then write two of the complete phrases in sentences of your own.
bullets: make · do · take · have · get
Endings: a) your best  b) a noise  c) angry  d) medicine  e) a look
make ____    do ____    take ____    have ____    get ____

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Write six sentences about yesterday and today using six different collocations from this worksheet. Underline the two words that go together.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: take a photograph; make a mistake; do your homework. have breakfast; have/take a shower; make the bed. get better; make a decision; take the bus. have a headache; do the washing-up; get married. make friends; get dressed; do your best.
1 made  2 gets  3 took  4 do  5 had  6 takes  7 done

1 does her homework  2 correct as written - *have a look* and *take a look* are both right, so accept it and say why  3 make a decision  4 caught/got a bad cold  5 have (or take) a shower  6 made friends
make b) a noise; do a) your best; take d) medicine; have e) a look; get c) angry. Sentences will vary.
Answers will vary. Check that both words of the pair are right, and that the tense fits: *I made a mistake*, not *I make a mistake*, about yesterday.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 30 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.

**Task 3 has a trap, deliberately.** Sentence 2 is already correct, and the class will change it anyway because the instruction says every sentence has a mistake. When they do, tell them the instruction was the trap: they must check the sentence, not obey the heading. That lesson transfers to every examination they sit.
**Record pairs, never single words.** Insist that notebooks show *make a mistake*, not *mistake*. This is the whole method, and five minutes spent enforcing it saves a year of *do a mistake*.

**The first language is the cause.** Most learners' languages use one verb where English uses two or three. Ask what *make* and *do* both translate to in their language - the answer explains their errors and makes them easier to accept.
**Drill aloud before writing.** *Make a mistake, do the shopping, take a photo* - said three times each, quickly, is worth more than a written exercise for phrases this fixed.
**Extension:** a collocation wall. One verb a week; learners add a phrase whenever they meet one, and wrong pairs come down with the class deciding why.

hero.text: A printable B1 vocabulary worksheet on word formation: building nouns, adjectives, adverbs and opposites from a root word. Five tasks, a full answer key and teacher's notes.

blocks.heading: About this worksheet
text: Word formation is the cheapest vocabulary a learner will ever buy. One known root - *care* - becomes *careful, carefully, careless, carelessly, carelessness*, and each of those is a mark in a word-formation question and a sentence the learner can now write.

blocks.label: Print this worksheet
blocks.note: Prints without the site's menus or advertisements.

blocks.title: Vocabulary: Word Formation · Level B1 · About 45 minutes
The four endings that do most of the work
text: Most word-formation answers come from a small set of endings.
**Nouns: -ion, -ment, -ness, -ity.** They make nouns from verbs and adjectives: *decide - decision, agree - agreement, happy - happiness, able - ability*.
**Adjectives: -ful, -less, -able.** *-ful* and *-less* make opposite adjectives from the same noun - *care - careful - careless*; *-able* means *can be done*: *wash - washable*.
**Adverbs: -ly.** It turns most adjectives into adverbs - *quick - quickly* - and note the spelling change in *happy - happily*.
**Opposites: un-, in-, im-, dis-.** Which prefix a word takes has to be learnt with the word: *unhappy, incorrect, impossible, disagree*.
Learn a root as a family, not as one word, and write the whole family in your notebook the first time you meet any member of it.

blocks.heading: Task 1. Complete the word families
text: Write the missing words. Some boxes have no common word - write a dash.
Example: decide → noun: **decision** · adjective: ____ · adverb: ____
bullets: care → noun: care · adjective (positive): ________ · adjective (negative): ________ · adverb (negative): ________
happy → noun: ________ · adverb: ________ · opposite adjective: ________
succeed → noun: ________ · adjective: ________ · adverb: ________
danger → adjective: ________ · adverb: ________
agree → noun: ________ · opposite verb: ________ · noun of the opposite: ________

blocks.heading: Task 2. Put the right form in the gap
text: Use the word in CAPITALS at the end of the line. Change its form.
Example: Her handwriting is almost unreadable. (READ)
bullets: The bus service in our town is very ________ . You can never be sure it will come. (RELY)
He gave a long ________ for being late, but nobody believed it. (EXPLAIN)
It was ________ of you to leave the gate open. (CARE)
She spoke so ________ that we could hear every word at the back. (CLEAR)
The new machine has made the old one completely ________ . (USE)
There is a real ________ that the match will be cancelled. (POSSIBLE)

blocks.heading: Task 3. Choose the right opposite
text: Add un-, in-, im- or dis- to make the opposite. Write the whole word.
Example: honest → **dishonest**
bullets: possible → ________
correct → ________
comfortable → ________
appear → ________
patient → ________
expensive → ________

blocks.heading: Task 4. Find and correct the mistake
text: Each sentence has one wrong word form. Cross it out and write the correct form.
Example: He drives very ~~careful~~ **carefully** in the rain.
bullets: My brother is a very success businessman. ________
The children were very excite about the trip. ________
Thank you for your kindly letter. ________
We waited for two hours, which was very annoyed. ________
She answered all the questions correct. ________

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn
text: Choose four of these roots - help, hope, use, friend, thought, comfort. For each one, write the word family you know and then one sentence using a form you did not know before today.

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: 1 careful; careless; carelessly.  2 happiness; happily; unhappy.  3 success; successful; successfully.  4 dangerous; dangerously.  5 agreement; disagree; disagreement.
1 unreliable  2 explanation  3 careless  4 clearly  5 useless  6 possibility
1 impossible  2 incorrect  3 uncomfortable  4 disappear  5 impatient  6 inexpensive
Answers will vary. Check that the form in the sentence matches its job: a noun after *a* or *the*, an adverb next to a verb, an adjective before a noun.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 35 minutes; Task 5 about 10, or set it as homework.

**Teach the job, not the ending.** Before Task 2, ask for each gap: *what kind of word do we need here - a thing, a describing word, or a word about how?* Learners who ask that question first get word-formation questions right even with an ending they have never seen.
**Task 3 has no rule.** Which prefix a word takes is learnt with the word. Do not let learners hunt for a pattern - ask them to record the opposite in their notebook beside the word from now on.
**Task 4 targets the two commonest mistakes** at B1: an adjective where an adverb belongs (*correct* for *correctly*), and -ed for -ing (*annoyed* for *annoying*). Both are worth naming out loud.
**Spelling matters here.** *Happy - happily*, *possible - possibility*, *rely - reliable*: half the lost marks in word formation are spelling, not word choice.
**Extension:** keep a word-family wall. One root a lesson, written up with its whole family, and learners add a sentence when they meet a new member of it.

pages.title: Writing: A Short Message Worksheet (A2)
pages.metaTitle: Free Short Message Writing Worksheet (A2) with Answers
pages.description: Free A2 writing worksheet on short messages and notes: the three parts, useful phrases, two models to study and three writing tasks, with an answer key.
pages.keywords: A2 writing worksheet, short message writing ESL, writing a note in English worksheet, elementary writing practice with model, invitation and apology message
pages.teaches: Writing short messages and notes in English at CEFR A2

hero.text: A printable A2 writing worksheet on the short message: the three parts every note needs, the phrases that carry them, two models to study, and three short writing tasks with a checklist. Full answer key and teacher's notes.

blocks.heading: About this worksheet
text: A short message is the first piece of real writing most learners will ever send in English, and it is what A2 examinations ask for: 35 to 45 words, three things to say, and nothing else.

blocks.label: Print this worksheet
blocks.note: Prints without the site's menus or advertisements.

blocks.title: Writing: A Short Message · Level A2 · About 40 minutes
The three parts of a short message
text: A note or message has three parts and about 35 to 45 words. Say who it is to, say your three things, and sign it.
**1. Who it is to.** *Hi Ama, / Dear Mr Silva, / To everyone in the class,*

**2. The three things.** An A2 task nearly always tells you exactly what to include - *say why you cannot come, suggest another day, and ask about the homework*. Write one sentence for each, in that order. Three sentences is enough; the mark is for covering all three, not for length.
**3. The ending.** *See you soon. / Thanks! / Let me know.* Then your name.

**Useful phrases.** Apologising: *I'm sorry, but ... / I'm afraid I can't ...* Inviting: *Would you like to ...? / Do you want to come ...?* Suggesting: *How about Friday? / Shall we meet at six?* Asking: *Could you tell me ...? / Can you bring ...?* Thanking: *Thanks for ... / It was very kind of you.*

blocks.heading: Task 1. Find the three things
text: Read the task, then underline the three things the message must include. Write them as a short list.
bullets: **Task A:** *Write a message to your friend Ravi. Tell him you cannot come to his party, explain why, and invite him to your house next week.* → Three things: **1 cannot come  2 why  3 invitation**
**Task B:** *Write a message to your teacher. Say you were absent yesterday, say why, and ask what homework you missed.* → 1 ________ 2 ________ 3 ________
**Task C:** *Write a message to a neighbour. Thank her for looking after your cat, say what you brought her from your trip, and invite her for tea on Sunday.* → 1 ________ 2 ________ 3 ________

blocks.heading: Task 2. Study the models
text: Read the two models. Write A, B or C beside each one to show which task above it answers. Then count the words, and underline one useful phrase in each.
bullets: *Hi Ravi, I'm really sorry, but I can't come to your party on Saturday. My aunt is arriving from Jaffna that day and I have to meet her at the station. Would you like to come to my house next Friday instead? Let me know! Nimali* → Task ____  Words: ____
*Dear Mr Silva, I'm sorry I was absent yesterday. I had a high fever and my mother took me to the doctor. Could you tell me what homework I missed, please? Thank you. Dinesh* → Task ____  Words: ____

blocks.heading: Task 3. Make it shorter
text: This message is too long and one sentence is not needed. Cross out the sentence that does not answer the task, then rewrite the message in 40 words or fewer.
bullets: **The task:** *Write to your friend. Say you found her umbrella, say where it is now, and arrange to give it back.*

*Hi Sanduni, How are you? I hope your family is well. I have some good news for you. After the class on Monday I was walking to the bus stop and I saw an umbrella under the desk in Room 4, and I think it is yours because it is blue with white flowers, and you had one like that last week. I have got it at my house now and it is safe. My brother says the handle is broken but I do not think so. Shall we meet at the library on Saturday at ten o'clock? I can bring it then. Malithi*

blocks.heading: Task 4. Your turn
text: Write a message for Task C above, in 35 to 45 words. Use one phrase for thanking and one for inviting.

blocks.heading: Task 5. Check your work
text: Tick each line. Then swap with a partner and check theirs.
bullets: Did I say who it is to, and sign my name? ____
Did I include all three things the task asked for? ____
Is it between 35 and 45 words? (Count them.) ____
Did I use at least one phrase from the box? ____
Is every sentence about something the task asked for? ____
Capital letters and full stops in the right places? ____

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: Task B: 1 say you were absent yesterday, 2 say why, 3 ask what homework you missed. Task C: 1 thank her for looking after the cat, 2 say what you brought her, 3 invite her for tea on Sunday.
Model 1 = Task A, 44 words. Model 2 = Task B, 38 words. Useful phrases: *I'm really sorry, but ... / Would you like to ...?* and *I'm sorry I was ... / Could you tell me ...?*

The unnecessary sentence is about the broken handle - the task did not ask about it. A model answer of 38 words: *Hi Sanduni, I found your blue umbrella under a desk in Room 4 after Monday's class. It's at my house now. Shall we meet at the library on Saturday at ten? I can bring it then. Malithi*

Answers will vary. A model of 41 words: *Dear Mrs Fernando, Thank you very much for looking after our cat while we were away. It was very kind of you. I brought you some tea from Nuwara Eliya. Would you like to come for tea on Sunday? Anjali*
Self-check. The three most commonly missed are the third point of the task, the word count, and the signature.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 3 take about 25 minutes; Tasks 4 and 5 about 15.

**Task 1 is the one that earns the marks.** Learners lose more at A2 for missing one of the three points than for any grammar mistake. Underlining the three things before writing takes thirty seconds and fixes most of it.

**Task 3 teaches what to leave out,** which is harder at A2 than what to put in. Learners write *How are you? I hope your family is well* out of politeness and then run out of words for the third point.
**Teach word counting properly:** count the words of one line, multiply by the number of lines. Learners will actually do this; counting to 45 one by one, they will not.
**Let them write the second one by hand on a real slip of paper** and deliver it to the person it is addressed to. A message with a reader is a different task from a message with a marker.
**Extension:** each learner writes a task (three things) for a partner, swaps, and marks the reply against the Task 5 checklist. Writing the task teaches the structure as well as answering one.

pages.description: Free B1 worksheet on writing an informal email: the four parts, formal phrases swapped for natural ones, a model to study, and a marking checklist.
pages.keywords: informal email worksheet ESL, how to write an informal email B1, email writing practice English, informal letter phrases worksheet, B1 writing worksheet with model
pages.teaches: Writing an informal email in English at CEFR B1

hero.text: A printable B1 writing worksheet on the informal email: the four parts, the opening and closing phrases that carry it, formal words swapped for natural ones, a model to study and a full writing task with a marking checklist.

blocks.heading: About this worksheet
text: Almost every B1 examination asks for one, and almost every learner writes it as a letter from 1950. The fix is a set of phrases and a shape, both of which are on this sheet.

blocks.label: Print this worksheet
blocks.note: Prints without the site's menus or advertisements.

blocks.title: Writing: An Informal Email · Level B1 · About 50 minutes
The shape of an informal email
text: An informal email to a friend has four parts and about 120 to 150 words.

**1. The greeting and opening line.** *Hi Nadun, / Hi there,* then something friendly - *Thanks for your email. Sorry I haven't written for so long. How are things?* Never begin with *I am writing to inform you*, which belongs in a formal letter.
**2. The reason.** Why you are writing, in one or two sentences - *I wanted to tell you about ... / Guess what?*

**3. The middle.** The news, the answers to their questions, or the invitation, with a reason or a detail for each thing you say. If their email asked you three questions, answer all three; examiners count them.
**4. The ending.** A forward-looking line and a sign-off - *Let me know what you think. Write soon. Hope to hear from you. Take care, / See you soon, / Love,* then your first name.
Contractions are normal throughout: *I'm, don't, can't, it's*. Short paragraphs, one idea each, and a blank line between them.

blocks.heading: Task 1. Put the email in order
text: Number the lines 1 to 8 to make a complete email.
bullets: ____ Anyway, I have to go now - my mother is calling me for dinner.
____ Hi Tharu,
____ Write soon and tell me about your new school.
____ Thanks for your email, and sorry for the late reply.
____ Love,  Kavi
____ The reason I'm writing is that we've moved house!
____ It's a lot smaller than the old one, but there's a big mango tree in the garden and my room has a window facing the road.
____ How are things with you?

blocks.heading: Task 2. Too formal - make it friendly
text: Rewrite each sentence as you would write it to a friend.
Example: I am writing to inform you that I have arrived. → **Just to let you know I've arrived!**
bullets: I regret to inform you that I shall be unable to attend. ____________________
I would be grateful if you could inform me of the date. ____________________
Please find attached a photograph of the house. ____________________
I look forward to receiving your response in due course. ____________________
I trust this email finds you in good health. ____________________

blocks.heading: Task 3. Answer all the questions
text: Read your friend's email, then write the one sentence you would use to answer each question. Do not write the whole email yet.
bullets: Your friend writes: *How was your trip to Ella? Who did you go with? Is it worth going in December, do you think? And did you take that camera you bought?*

blocks.heading: Task 4. Study the model, then find the four parts
text: Read the model below. Write G (greeting and opening), R (reason), M (middle) or E (ending) beside each paragraph, and underline every contraction.
bullets: *Hi Sanuli,*  *Thanks for your message - it was lovely to hear from you. Sorry I've taken a week to reply; things have been busy here.*  → ____
*I'm writing because I've got some news: I've finally started the photography course I told you about.*  → ____

*It's every Saturday morning for three months, and there are only eight of us in the group, so we get a lot of attention. Last week we spent two hours photographing the fish market, which sounds strange but was the best class so far. The teacher says I need to stop using the flash, which I'm sure is true.*  → ____
*Anyway, tell me how the new job is going. Are you still working late every evening? Let me know if you're free on a Sunday and we'll meet.*  *Take care,*  *Ishan*  → ____

blocks.heading: Task 5. Your turn: write the email
text: Your friend has written asking about a course, a club or a trip you have started or taken. Reply in 120 to 150 words. Use the four parts, at least four contractions, and at least two of the phrases from the box. Then check your work against the list below.
bullets: **Plan first, in four lines:** greeting and opening phrase · reason for writing · two things for the middle, each with a detail · closing line and sign-off

**Check before you hand it in.** Tick each one: (1) Did I answer everything my friend asked? (2) Is there a blank line between paragraphs? (3) Did I use contractions? (4) Did I avoid *I am writing to inform you*? (5) Is it between 120 and 150 words? (6) Did I sign off with my first name?

blocks.heading: For the teacher: answer key
rows: 1 Hi Tharu,  2 Thanks for your email, and sorry for the late reply.  3 How are things with you?  4 The reason I'm writing is that we've moved house!  5 It's a lot smaller than the old one ...  6 Anyway, I have to go now ...  7 Write soon and tell me about your new school.  8 Love, Kavi

Suggested answers. 1 I'm really sorry, but I can't come. 2 Could you let me know the date? 3 Here's a photo of the house. 4 Let me know what you think. / Hope to hear from you soon. 5 Hope you're well.
Answers will vary. Check that there are four answers and that each one is a full sentence. Learners who answer three out of four are making the commonest examination mistake in this task.

Paragraph 1 = G; paragraph 2 = R; paragraph 3 = M; paragraph 4 = E. Contractions: it was (none), I've, I'm, I've, It's, I'm, you're, we'll - eight in total, which is what a natural informal email looks like.

Answers will vary. Mark on four things: all questions answered; the four parts present; informal register including contractions; length within 120 to 150 words. Grammar and spelling matter, but at B1 the register and the completeness carry most of the marks.

blocks.heading: Teacher's notes
bullets: **Timing:** Tasks 1 to 4 take about 30 minutes; Task 5 needs 20, or set the writing as homework and do the checklist in the next lesson.

**Do not skip Task 3.** Not answering every question is the single most expensive mistake in this task type, and it costs marks even when the English is good. Make learners underline the questions in the prompt before they write anything.

**Register is teachable in five minutes.** Put *I am writing to inform you* and *Just to let you know* side by side on the board and ask which one a friend would send. Learners over-formalise because they were taught letters first, not because they cannot hear the difference.
**Contractions are not optional here.** An informal email without them reads wrong to an examiner. Counting them in Task 4 makes the point better than telling them.
**Word count:** teach learners to count the words of one full line and multiply, rather than counting all 150. It takes ten seconds and they will actually do it.

**Peer marking works well with Task 5.** Learners swap and mark against the six-point checklist only - no other corrections. They find missing questions and missing paragraphs faster than a teacher reading thirty papers.
**Extension:** the same news, written as a formal email to a course tutor. Putting the two side by side is the clearest register lesson available.

pages.title: 18 ESL Classroom Games That Teach Something
pages.metaTitle: 18 ESL Classroom Games That Teach Something (A1-B2)
pages.description: 18 free ESL classroom games for A1 to B2: the language point each one practises, numbered steps, a variation, and a note for classes of 40 or more.
pages.keywords: ESL classroom games, English games for the classroom, EFL games for adults, vocabulary games for English class, grammar games ESL, games for large English classes, no-materials ESL games
pages.teaches: Vocabulary, grammar and fluency through classroom games

hero.text: Eighteen games, each aimed at a language point rather than at filling five minutes. Every one says what it practises, how long it takes, what you need and how to run it in a class of forty.

blocks.heading: About these activities
text: They are grouped by what they are for: vocabulary, grammar, speaking and whole-class energy. Nothing here needs a projector, and most need nothing at all.

blocks.heading: What makes a classroom game worth the time
bullets: **A game needs a language point, or it is a break.** Before you play, be able to finish this sentence: *while they play this, learners are practising ...* If you cannot, the game is entertainment, which is fine at the end of term and expensive in week three.

**Everybody plays at once, or almost nobody plays.** A game where two learners compete at the front while thirty-eight watch gives two learners practice. Teams, pairs and simultaneous rounds are what make a game work in a real class.
**Teach the language of the game first.** *It's my turn. You missed. Whose turn is it? That's not fair!* Five minutes spent on these, once, pays back all year.
**Short and stopped early.** Three minutes of a fast game beats ten minutes of the same game dying. Stop while they still want to play.
**Keep the scoring simple and the teams equal.** Long scoring arguments take the lesson. Two teams, points on the board, no half points.

**Decide beforehand what happens to mistakes.** For fluency games, note errors and deal with them afterwards. For accuracy games, a wrong sentence loses the point - that is the game's own correction, and it stings less than yours.

blocks.heading: Vocabulary games
text: For learning, recycling and testing words - the part of language that most needs repetition.

blocks.name: The word wall race
blocks.language: Any word set: food, jobs, verbs, adjectives
steps: Name a category: *things in a kitchen.* Each team has two minutes to write as many as they can.
Teams swap lists and check each other's spelling; a misspelt word scores nothing.
One point per correct word, two for a word no other team has.
Board the best five words for the class to copy.
blocks.variation: Harder: every word must begin with the same letter, or have two syllables.
blocks.bigClass: Four teams by rows; each row passes one sheet along, which also stops one learner writing everything.

blocks.name: Definition bingo
blocks.language: Listening to definitions; the vocabulary of one unit
steps: Board twelve words from recent lessons. Each learner draws a grid of six squares and writes any six of the twelve in it.
Read out definitions in random order, in your own words. Learners cross off a word when they recognise its definition.
The first with all six shouts bingo and must read back the six words with their meanings - that check is the point of the game.
Play a second round with the learners writing and reading the definitions.
blocks.variation: Read example sentences with the word missing instead of definitions.
blocks.bigClass: Perfect for a large class: everyone plays at once and you speak only once per item.

blocks.name: Odd one out
blocks.language: Categories, reasons, *because*
steps: Write four words on the board: *apple, banana, carrot, mango.*
Pairs choose the odd one and give a reason. Any answer with a good reason scores.
Take two or three different answers: the reasoning is the language, not the choice.
Learners write the next set for the class.
blocks.variation: Verbs instead of nouns: *run, swim, read, jump.*
blocks.bigClass: Whole class works from the board; hear four reasons.

blocks.name: The memory tray
blocks.prep: Ten small objects, or ten words on the board
blocks.language: *There was / there were*; plurals; *I think there was ...*
steps: Show ten objects for thirty seconds, then cover them.
In pairs, learners list everything they remember, in full sentences: *There was a red pen.*
Uncover and check. One point per correct item, none for a list without a sentence.
Play a second round with two objects changed, and ask what is different.
blocks.variation: No objects: ten words on the board, rubbed out after thirty seconds.
blocks.bigClass: Words on the board work for any class size; objects only for small rooms.

blocks.name: Word tennis
blocks.language: Rapid recall of one word set
steps: Name a category. Partners say words alternately, one each, with no repeats and no long pauses.
A learner who repeats or pauses loses the point; start a new category.
Three categories is enough.
Use the category you taught last lesson, and it becomes revision.
blocks.variation: Harder version: each word must begin with the last letter of the previous one.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed - everyone plays in pairs at once.

blocks.heading: Grammar games
text: Accuracy practice that does not feel like a worksheet.

blocks.name: Sentence auction
blocks.prep: Ten sentences, half of them wrong
blocks.language: Whatever grammar you have taught: tenses, articles, word order
steps: Each team has an imaginary 100 points. Read out or board ten sentences, half correct and half not.
Teams bid points on the sentences they believe are correct.
Reveal after each one: a correct sentence wins the bid back doubled, a wrong one loses it.
The team with most points explains two of the corrections.
blocks.variation: Use sentences you collected from the class's own writing, unnamed.
blocks.bigClass: Teams by rows; bids written on paper and held up together, so nobody can hear the others first.

blocks.name: Beat the teacher
blocks.language: Any target structure
steps: You say a sentence using the target structure. Sometimes it is wrong.
The class wins a point for spotting a mistake, and you win one for every mistake that passes.
Learners must say what is wrong and correct it, not just shout.
Six or eight sentences is enough.
blocks.variation: Let a learner take your place once the class knows the game.
blocks.bigClass: Works best with a big class - the whole room can answer together.

blocks.name: Running dictation
blocks.prep: One short text on the wall, or on the board at the back
blocks.language: Any grammar in a text; spelling; listening and reading
steps: Put the text where learners must walk to read it: the back wall, the corridor door.
One learner walks, reads and remembers a piece; the other writes what they hear. No paper travels.
Halfway through, they swap roles.
The pair with the most accurate text wins - accuracy, not speed.
blocks.variation: Use a text with the target grammar in every sentence, and check those words most carefully.
blocks.bigClass: Two copies on two walls. Where learners cannot move, the reader turns round and whispers from memory instead.

blocks.name: Question basketball
blocks.prep: A ball or a rolled paper, and a bin
blocks.language: Question forms in any tense
steps: A team earns a throw by asking a correct question about a prompt you give: *the weekend, your family, last holiday.*
The question must be grammatically correct, or no throw.
One point for the question, two more for the throw that goes in.
Change the tense each round.
blocks.variation: No ball: the throw is replaced by a spelling challenge for the bonus points.
blocks.bigClass: Two teams of twenty; one thrower per round, chosen by the team in turn, so everyone gets a go over a term.

blocks.name: Grammar stations
blocks.prep: Four sheets, one on each desk group
blocks.language: Four different structures, revised in one lesson
steps: Four desks each have a different short task: a gap fill, a correction, a transformation, a question-writing task.
Groups have three minutes at each, then rotate.
The last group at each station reads the answers out; earlier groups check their own.
Nobody sits still for more than three minutes, which is why it works after lunch.
blocks.variation: Station five: write the fifth task for next time.
blocks.bigClass: Eight stations, two copies of each task; groups rotate within their half of the room.

blocks.heading: Games that make them speak
text: Fluency games with a rule that forces the target language out.

blocks.name: The yes-no game
blocks.language: Question forms; avoiding yes and no; short answers
steps: One learner answers questions for sixty seconds without saying yes or no.
The partner asks anything, trying to trap them: *Are you a student? You live here, don't you?*
Teach the escape phrases first: *That's right. Not at all. I'm afraid so. Possibly.*
Swap, and see who lasts longer.
blocks.variation: Ban *maybe* as well, once the class is good at it.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.name: Liar's interview
blocks.language: Past simple questions; consistency in answers
steps: One learner claims an unusual experience: *I have met a famous singer.* It may be true or invented.
The group has two minutes of questions to decide.
The group votes, then the truth comes out. A convincing liar and a sharp group both score.
Everyone takes a turn.
blocks.variation: The teacher goes first with a true story nobody believes.
blocks.bigClass: All groups at once; no reporting stage needed.

blocks.name: The silent film
blocks.language: Present continuous for actions happening now; adverbs
steps: Two learners in each group mime a short everyday scene - missing a bus, cooking badly, a first day at work - with no sound at all.
The other two narrate it aloud as it happens: *He's running. Now she's laughing at him.*
Swap roles and mime a new scene.
The rule that makes it work: narrators must speak continuously, so hesitation costs the group its turn.
blocks.variation: Narrate afterwards in the past simple instead, which turns it into a storytelling task.
blocks.bigClass: All groups play at once; two groups perform for the class at the end if there is time.

blocks.name: The one-minute story
blocks.language: Narrative tenses; sequencing
steps: Give three words that must appear: *a key, a storm, a stranger.*
Each group has three minutes to agree a story, then one minute to tell it.
The listening groups hold up a hand when they hear each of the three words.
Best story, by vote, not by teacher.
blocks.variation: Each group passes its three words to the next group.
blocks.bigClass: Groups tell their story to one other group rather than to the class.

blocks.heading: Five-minute energy games
text: For the moment when the class stops listening, with just enough language to justify them.

blocks.name: Right or wrong, on your feet
blocks.language: True/false statements; any grammar point
steps: Say a sentence. Learners stand if it is grammatically correct and stay seated if it is not.
Anyone who moves late or wrongly sits out one round.
Eight sentences, fast.
It tells you in two minutes who has understood a grammar point, which is why it beats asking.
blocks.variation: True/false about the class's own reading text instead.
blocks.bigClass: Better with a big class: you can see the whole room decide.

blocks.name: The alphabet chain
blocks.language: Vocabulary recall; alphabet; spelling
steps: Name a category. Each learner in turn says a word beginning with the next letter of the alphabet.
A learner who cannot, passes; the row loses a point.
Go round twice with different categories.
Say the letters aloud as you go, so the alphabet itself gets practised.
blocks.variation: Backwards from Z for a class that finds it too easy.
blocks.bigClass: Row against row keeps it moving in a class of any size.

blocks.name: Change places if
blocks.prep: Chairs in a circle, if possible
blocks.language: Present and past simple; *if* clauses
steps: One learner in the middle says: *Change places if you walked to school today.*
Everyone it is true for moves; the one left without a seat goes to the middle.
Teach the sentence pattern first and leave it on the board.
Six or seven rounds.
blocks.variation: Where chairs cannot move: learners stand and sit instead of changing seats.
blocks.bigClass: Do it in two halves of the room simultaneously, with one learner in the middle of each.

blocks.name: Board race
blocks.language: Spelling; word order; any short answer
steps: Two learners at the board, one from each team.
Say a word to spell, or a jumbled sentence to write in order. First correct answer wins the point.
Change the writers every round so everyone takes a turn.
Insist the answer is correct, not just first, or the game teaches speed instead of English.
blocks.variation: Three teams if the board is wide enough.
blocks.bigClass: The rest of the class writes the same answer in their notebooks, so nobody is only watching.

items.title: Are games not just a waste of teaching time?
text: A game with a language point is practice with the attention on meaning, which is when language sticks. Describe it, do not say it drills defining language harder than any exercise. The waste is a game with no language point, played because the lesson ran short.

items.title: My class becomes uncontrollable during games.
text: Three fixes, in order: shorter rounds; teams rather than individuals; and a clear stop signal agreed and practised before you start. A game that ends while it is still enjoyable does not need controlling.

items.title: I have forty-five learners and fixed desks. Which games work?
text: Every game here has a line for large classes. The safest are Beat the teacher, Right or wrong on your feet, Word tennis, Sentence auction and Board race with the class writing along - none need anyone to move.

items.title: How do I stop the same learners winning every time?
text: Make teams, not individuals, and change them weekly. Score for things other than speed: best reason, best spelling, most words nobody else had. Then the strongest learner cannot carry every round.

items.title: Should I correct mistakes during a game?
text: In accuracy games, a wrong answer simply loses the point, and that is correction enough. In fluency games, note the errors and put four sentences on the board afterwards for the class to repair.

pages.title: 12 Sets of English Conversation Questions, by Topic
pages.metaTitle: 12 Sets of English Conversation Questions, by Topic (A2-B2)
pages.description: 12 sets of conversation questions for A2-B2 ESL classes: the language each one practises, numbered steps, a variation, and a note for classes of 40 or more.
pages.keywords: ESL conversation questions, English conversation questions by topic, speaking questions for English class, discussion questions ESL, conversation topics for adults learning English
pages.teaches: Conversation practice by topic

hero.text: Twelve sets of conversation questions, graded from A2 to B2, with the language each topic needs and a way to run it that keeps everyone talking rather than one confident learner answering everything.

blocks.heading: About these activities
text: Every set gives easier and harder questions, so one page serves a mixed class. The topics are ones any class in any country can discuss safely.

blocks.heading: Making conversation questions actually work
bullets: **Never ask the whole class a conversation question.** One learner answers, thirty listen. Put the questions in pairs or threes, and move round.
**Give the answering language, not just the question.** Two or three phrases on the board - *It depends. I'd say ... The thing is ...* - turn one-word answers into conversations.
**Let them choose.** Pairs pick four questions from the set rather than working through all of them. Choice raises the quality of the answers.
**Thirty seconds of silent thinking first.** With questions of opinion, this is the difference between a real answer and "I don't know".
**Ask for a follow-up, always.** The rule "you must ask one more question after each answer" is what makes it a conversation rather than an interview.
**Change partners once.** The second telling is always better than the first, which is where the fluency gain comes from.

blocks.heading: Everyday life (A2)
text: Concrete topics with simple tenses: safe ground for a class that has not talked much before.

blocks.name: Food and meals
blocks.language: Present simple; *like / prefer*; frequency; food vocabulary
steps: **Easier:** What do you usually have for breakfast? Who cooks in your home? What food do you eat every week? Is there a food you really do not like?
**Harder:** What dish would you cook for a visitor from another country, and why? Has your diet changed in the last five years? Should schools decide what children eat?
Put three phrases on the board first: *It depends. I'd rather ... To be honest, ...*
Pairs choose four questions; after each answer the partner must ask one more question.
blocks.variation: Each learner describes one dish in detail without naming it; the partner guesses.
blocks.bigClass: Pairs throughout; hear three answers at the end, not thirty.

blocks.name: Home and where you live
blocks.language: *There is / there are*; prepositions; comparatives
steps: **Easier:** Where do you live? What is near your home? What is the best thing about your area? Do you prefer a city or the countryside?
**Harder:** What would you change about your town? Is it better to live where you grew up or to move away? What makes a place feel like home?
Give the comparative forms on the board if the class is A2.
After four questions, learners change partners and answer two of them again - better the second time.
blocks.variation: Learners draw their ideal home in two minutes and describe it to a partner.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.name: Free time and weekends
blocks.language: Present simple; past simple; *enjoy / prefer* + -ing
steps: **Easier:** What do you do at the weekend? What did you do last Saturday? Do you prefer doing things alone or with other people?
**Harder:** Has the way people spend free time changed since your parents were young? Is being busy a good thing? What would you do with one completely free day?
Pairs first, then join two pairs and compare answers to the last question.
One learner from each four reports the most interesting answer.
blocks.variation: Rank five free-time activities and agree an order in the group of four.
blocks.bigClass: The join-into-fours step works with any class size; nobody presents from the front.

blocks.heading: People and experience (B1)
text: Personal but safe: nothing here asks a learner to reveal family or money troubles.

blocks.name: Friends
blocks.language: Present perfect; *know / meet*; adjectives of character
steps: **Easier:** How did you meet your best friend? What makes a good friend? How often do you see your friends?
**Harder:** Is it possible to be real friends with someone you have never met in person? Do friendships change when people move away? Can a friend be too honest?
Board four character adjectives before you start, and require one in every answer.
Pairs choose four questions; partner asks one follow-up each time.
blocks.variation: Each learner describes a friend without naming them; the class guesses whether they are older or younger.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.name: Travel and journeys
blocks.language: Present perfect for experience; past simple for detail
steps: **Easier:** Have you ever travelled by train? What is the longest journey you have made? Where would you like to go?
**Harder:** Does travel really change people, or only the photographs they have? What is the difference between a traveller and a tourist? Should there be limits on flying?
Point out the pattern: the present perfect asks, the past simple answers - *Have you ever been to ...? Yes, I went in 2019.*
After four questions, change partners and retell one of your partner's answers.
blocks.variation: Plan a two-day trip for your partner based on what they said.
blocks.bigClass: Pairs; hear two retellings.

blocks.name: Learning English
blocks.language: *used to*; comparatives; *find it easy/hard to ...*
steps: **Easier:** How long have you studied English? What is easy for you? What is hard? Where do you use English outside class?
**Harder:** What is the fastest way to improve speaking? Does your first language help or get in the way? Should everyone learn a second language at school?
Collect the best advice on the board as a class list at the end - it becomes a poster for the room.
This set is worth doing in the first week of a course and again in the last.
blocks.variation: Learners write one piece of advice for a learner one level below them.
blocks.bigClass: The class list at the end is the whole-class stage; the talking stays in pairs.

blocks.heading: Opinions and ideas (B1 to B2)
text: For classes that can hold a position and give a reason. Safe subjects, real disagreement.

blocks.name: Technology and phones
blocks.language: *Should*; *would*; agreeing and disagreeing
steps: **Easier:** How long do you use your phone each day? What do you use it for most? Could you live without it for a week?
**Harder:** Should phones be allowed in schools? Has technology made people better at communicating, or worse? What should children not be allowed to do online?
Board three phrases for disagreeing politely: *I see your point, but ... That depends on ... I'm not so sure.*
Pairs discuss, then fours try to agree one answer to the second harder question.
blocks.variation: Take a vote before and after the discussion, and see whether anyone changed their mind.
blocks.bigClass: The fours stage needs no space and no presenting.

blocks.name: Work and jobs
blocks.language: Future forms; conditionals; job vocabulary
steps: **Easier:** What job would you like? What jobs are common in your area? What makes a job good?
**Harder:** Is it better to have work you love or work that pays well? Will people still do the same jobs in twenty years? Should everybody retire at the same age?
Avoid asking what learners' parents earn or do, which is not safe ground in every class.
Pairs choose four questions and must reach a conclusion, not just exchange views.
blocks.variation: Each pair invents a job that will exist in 2050 and explains it.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.name: School and learning
blocks.language: *Should*; passive forms; giving examples
steps: **Easier:** What is your favourite subject and why? What time does your school day start? What would you change about it?
**Harder:** Are exams a fair way to measure what someone knows? Should students choose all their own subjects? Is homework useful?
Require one example from experience in each answer: *For example, last year we ...*
Groups of three so that a quiet learner can enter the conversation more easily than in a four.
blocks.variation: Groups write one new school rule and argue for it.
blocks.bigClass: Threes work at once; take three conclusions.

blocks.heading: Imagination and hypotheticals (B1 to B2)
text: Conditionals in real use, and the questions learners remember after the lesson.

blocks.name: If you could choose
blocks.language: Second conditional; *would*; reasons
steps: **Easier:** If you could visit any country, where would you go? If you had one free day, what would you do? If you could learn one new skill, what?
**Harder:** If you could change one decision you have made, would you? If you had to live in another century, which would you choose? If you could know one thing about the future, would you want to?
Drill the form once: *If + past, would + verb*. Beginners tend to answer with *will*.
Partner must ask *why* after every answer - the reason is where the language is.
blocks.variation: Answer as somebody else - a grandparent, a famous person - and the partner guesses who.
blocks.bigClass: No change needed.

blocks.name: Rules of a new country
blocks.language: *Must / mustn't*; *should*; obligation and permission
steps: Each group invents a small country and agrees five rules everyone must follow.
Two rules must be about school, and two about the environment.
Groups swap rules with another group and ask three hard questions about them.
Which country would the class prefer to live in?
blocks.variation: Each group also invents one rule that would be unpopular but useful.
blocks.bigClass: Swapping between neighbouring groups means nothing goes to the front.

blocks.name: Ten years from now
blocks.language: Future forms; *I hope to ...*; *I might ...*
steps: **Easier:** Where do you think you will live? What will you be doing? What will be the same?
**Harder:** What will have changed in your town? Will people read fewer books? What is one thing you hope will not change?
Teach the difference between *will* for prediction and *might* for possibility before they start.
Change partners once and report your first partner's answer to the new one.
blocks.variation: Write a two-sentence message to yourself in ten years, and read it to a partner.
blocks.bigClass: The change of partner works as "turn and face the row behind you".

items.title: Learners answer in one word and stop.
text: Two causes: the question had a yes/no answer, or they had no thinking time. Use questions that begin with *what, why, how*, give thirty seconds of silence first, and make the follow-up question a rule rather than a hope.

items.title: Can I use these with a mixed-level class?
text: That is why each set has easier and harder questions. Weaker pairs take the first group, stronger pairs the second, and the topic is the same across the room, so feedback at the end works for everybody.

items.title: Should I correct their English during a conversation?
text: No. Note what you hear and put four sentences on the board at the end for the class to repair, unnamed. Correcting mid-conversation teaches learners that speaking is dangerous.

items.title: How do I stop the confident ones dominating?
text: Give turns a shape: each learner answers one question fully before anyone answers a second; or in threes, one asks, one answers, one listens for the follow-up question and then swaps. Structure beats asking people to speak less.

items.title: How many questions should one lesson use?
text: Four, well answered, with follow-ups and a change of partner, is a better twenty minutes than twelve questions rushed.
